SB001.text: Null or invalid input causes no output / null output with no explicit error raised

SB002.text: Non-numeric or wrong-type input causes type mismatch / unexpected output

SB003.text: Zero or negative count/division/subdivision parameter produces degenerate or empty output

SB004.text: Data tree / list length mismatch between inputs causes unexpected branching or null items

SB005.text: Out-of-range numeric values (e.g., alpha/strength outside 0–1, angle outside valid bounds) clamp silently or produce unexpected results

SB006.text: Component with no inputs produces no output until data is bound or values set externally

SB007.text: Downstream type errors when output is connected to a component expecting a different type (float vs integer, generic vs specific)

SB008.text: Mesh input must be valid and non-empty; null or degenerate mesh produces no output

SB009.text: Curve input must be valid and non-null; degenerate or wrong curve type causes failure or empty output

SB010.text: Strength parameter of 0 disables the effect entirely; component produces no response

SB011.text: Silent failure / no warning raised when output is empty or data is lost

SB012.text: Colour component: disconnected or out-of-range channel inputs yield null or unexpected colour output

SB013.text: Math domain error: undefined operation (log of zero/negative, division by zero, negative base with fractional exponent) returns NaN or error

SB014.text: Min > Max or inverted range parameter causes invalid settings or unexpected output

SB015.text: Zero-length or parallel vectors cause degenerate plane/rotation failure

SB016.text: Kangaroo2 goal: input points must be ordered consistently; wrong ordering distorts constraint behavior

SB017.text: Boolean input unconnected uses default value that may differ from user intent

SB018.text: Surface input must be an actual surface type; passing other geometry types causes failure

SB019.text: Mismatched list lengths between paired inputs causes null items or truncated output

SB020.text: Open Brep used as cutter or splitter may not reliably split closed solids

SB021.text: Out-of-range integer index in pattern or topology output causes silent downstream errors

SB022.text: Curve-processing components fail or return degenerate results at inflection points, straight segments, or curvature singularities

SB023.text: Singular or non-invertible transform input causes null or failed output

SB024.text: Missing boundary anchors or constraints causes full mesh/geometry collapse during simulation

SB025.text: Plane mismatch between curve and constraint plane causes points to escape or project incorrectly

similar_pairs.reason: Both take Points and Strength as inputs, output Generic Data (S), and involve point-based collision detection against a boundary geometry. SphereCollide uses radius while SolidPointCollide uses a Mesh solid, but both fundamentally repel points from a surface/boundary.

Both take Points and Strength as inputs and output Generic Data (S). Both perform point collision goals — SphereCollide between point pairs with radius, CurvePointCollide between points and a curve boundary. Same output identifier 'S' suggests analogous goal type.

Both take Points, a boundary geometry (Mesh vs Curve), a Boolean 'In' flag to control inside/outside behavior, and Strength. Both output Generic Data 'S'. They are structurally nearly identical — one uses a mesh solid, the other a curve as the collision boundary. Same In/Strength/Points pattern.

Both involve curve geometry and a Plane input alongside Strength. Collide2d uses polylines in a plane for 2D collision, CurvePointCollide uses a curve with a plane for point-curve collision. Both are planar/curve-based collision goals.

Both output Generic Data labeled 'C' and take Strength as input. Both are general collision goals — Collide2d for 2D polyline collisions, Collider for general object collisions with radii. Same output name 'C' suggests they belong to the same collision goal category.

Both take Mesh geometry and Strength as inputs, outputting Generic Data. SoftBodyCollide works with meshes colliding against each other, SolidPointCollide uses a mesh as the collision solid. Both are mesh-based collision goals.
Both are colour selection UI components with no inputs, producing colour values. Colour Picker and Colour Wheel serve analogous roles as interactive colour input widgets.
Both Colour Picker and Colour Swatch are colour-related UI input components with no inputs, used to define or display colour values in a GH canvas.
Colour Wheel and Colour Swatch are both colour UI components with no inputs, providing colour data to downstream components.
Both Digit Scroller and Number Slider are numeric input UI widgets with no inputs that produce a numeric value. They serve the same role of providing user-controlled numeric input.
Digit Scroller and MD Slider are both slider-style numeric input components with no inputs, used to provide numeric or parameter values interactively.
Number Slider and MD Slider are both slider-based numeric input UI components with no inputs, providing user-controlled numeric values.
Number Slider and Value List are both UI input components with no inputs that provide selectable values to the canvas, serving as user-driven data sources.
Both Read File and Import 3DM take a file path (Text) as a primary input and output data from that file. They perform analogous file-reading operations, differing only in file format and output type.
Both Read File and Import PDB take a file path (Text F input) and output data read from that file. They share the same file-import pattern.

Both Import PDB and Import 3DM are file import components that take a file path (Text) as primary input and output geometric or structured data. They perform analogous import operations for different file formats.
Panel and Image Resource are both display/data-container UI components with no active inputs, used to present or hold static data (text or image) on the canvas.

Graph Mapper and Gradient both perform value-mapping operations: Graph Mapper maps numeric values through a curve function, while Gradient maps a numeric parameter t to a colour. Both transform numeric inputs into a remapped output.
Unweld Mesh and Weld Mesh are inverse operations with identical I/O signatures (Mesh + Number angle -> Mesh). Both operate on mesh edge normals using an angle threshold parameter.
Mesh Flip and Mesh UnifyNormals both take a single Mesh input and output a Mesh, and both operate on mesh face/vertex normals. They are closely related normal-correction operations.
Mesh Flip and Disjoint Mesh both take a single Mesh and output a single Mesh with identical minimal signatures, performing single-pass mesh topology modifications.
Mesh Flip and Mesh Join both have identical single-input/single-output Mesh signatures and perform mesh topology operations.
Mesh UnifyNormals and Disjoint Mesh both accept a single Mesh and return a single Mesh, performing single-pass structural mesh operations.
Disjoint Mesh and Mesh Join are conceptually inverse operations (splitting vs joining mesh parts) with identical I/O signatures (Mesh -> Mesh).
Cull Faces and Cull Vertices are analogous culling operations on mesh topology (faces vs vertices), both taking Mesh + Boolean pattern inputs and outputting Mesh.
Cull Faces and Delete Vertices are analogous removal operations on mesh elements (faces vs vertices), both outputting a modified Mesh.
Cull Vertices and Delete Vertices both remove vertices from a mesh using Boolean/index selection, outputting a modified Mesh.
Blur Mesh and Quadrangulate both take a Mesh plus a numeric/integer parameter and output a modified Mesh, performing iterative mesh refinement/modification operations.
Blur Mesh and Unweld Mesh both take a Mesh plus a single numeric parameter and output a Mesh, performing mesh attribute smoothing/modification operations.

Both Settings (Quality) and Settings (Speed) are mesh settings providers with identical I/O signatures: no inputs and a single MeshParameters output. They are analogous components offering different presets for the same parameter type, making them nearly identical structurally and semantically.

Both Mesh CullUnused Vertices and Triangulate take a single Mesh as input and produce a Mesh as primary output. Both perform mesh cleanup/normalization operations that transform mesh topology without requiring additional geometry inputs.

Both Mesh CullUnused Vertices and Flip Mesh take a Mesh as their primary input and output a Mesh. Both are mesh modification utilities that alter mesh properties (vertex/face data) without changing geometry type.
Both Flip Mesh and Triangulate accept a Mesh input and return a Mesh output. Both are mesh processing operations that restructure mesh face/vertex data.

Both are 'Get' type components retrieving typed values (Point vs Number) from context with identical no-input/no-output structure
Both are 'Get' type components retrieving primitive typed values (Boolean vs Number) from context; analogous operations on different primitive types
Both are 'Get' type components with no explicit inputs/outputs, retrieving specific typed data from context
Both are 'Get' type components retrieving data values from context with no explicit inputs/outputs

Both are data flow control components that buffer or record generic data passing through a pipeline; analogous data management roles
Both are text display/output components (Text Balloon vs Context Print) that present textual information; Context Print takes text input while Text Balloon displays inline
Both are parameter inspection/selection utility components (Param Viewer vs Cherry Picker) used to examine or extract data from parameter collections
Both are navigation/selection utility components with no explicit inputs/outputs used for data routing and access within the canvas

Both are 'Get' components that retrieve specific types of Rhino geometry/objects from the document. Get Plane and Get Object both serve as geometry acquisition utilities with no inputs, functioning as data sources.

Get Object and Get Geometry are nearly identical in purpose - both retrieve geometric data from the Rhino document with no inputs. Get Geometry is a more specific form of Get Object, both functioning as document geometry acquisition components.
Get Plane and Get Geometry are both 'Get' family components that retrieve specific geometric entities (plane vs geometry) from the Rhino document with no inputs required.
Sketch and Scribble are both freehand drawing/annotation utilities with no inputs or outputs, used for visual annotation within the Grasshopper canvas rather than computational geometry operations.

Both are object attribute components with an Integer 'S' (source/mode) parameter and passthrough IO pattern where inputs mirror outputs. Render Material deals with material assignment; Display Colour deals with colour assignment — both control visual appearance properties with the same selector integer pattern.

Both are object attribute selector components sharing an Integer 'S' parameter and identical passthrough IO structure (inputs == outputs). Both assign a specific attribute type (material vs linetype) to objects with a mode/source integer selector.

Both Object Linetype and Print Width are object attribute components with an Integer 'S' selector and passthrough IO pattern. Both deal with drafting/display properties (linetype vs print width) and follow the same structural pattern of attribute + integer source + value.
Both Display Colour and Print Width share Integer 'S' selector parameter and passthrough IO pattern. Both control visual/output display properties of objects with a mode selector integer.

Both Render Attributes and Drafting Attributes are attribute container components with passthrough IO (inputs mirror outputs). Both encapsulate a group of related display/rendering properties and share structural similarity as compound attribute holders.

Both Render Material and Render Attributes share the 'Om' (Object Material) parameter and passthrough IO pattern. They operate in the same rendering domain, with Render Attributes being a superset container that includes Object Material.
Both Object Linetype and Drafting Attributes share a linetype-related parameter ('L') and passthrough IO pattern. Both operate in the drafting/display domain controlling line appearance properties.

Both Colour XYZ and Colour LCH take 4 Number inputs (A + 3 channel values) and output a single Colour. They are analogous colour construction components using different colour spaces, sharing identical input/output structure.

Both Colour XYZ and Colour HSL take 4 Number inputs (A + 3 channel values) and output a single Colour. They are analogous colour construction components using different colour spaces, sharing identical input/output structure.

Both Colour LCH and Colour HSL take 4 Number inputs (A + 3 channel values) and output a single Colour. They are analogous colour construction components using different colour spaces, sharing identical input/output structure.

Both Text Tag and Text Tag 3D are annotation/display components that take a location, Text, and Colour inputs and produce no geometric output. Text Tag 3D extends Text Tag with a Plane instead of Point, plus size and justification parameters.

Both Serial Dimension and Circular Dimension are dimensioning annotation components that take Text (T) and Scale/Size (S as Number) inputs and produce no output. Both are used to annotate geometry with measurements.

Symbol (Simple) produces a Symbol Display output (D) and Symbol Display consumes that exact Symbol Display type along with a Point. They form a producer-consumer pair for the same data type, making them semantically coupled display components.
Both Blend Colours and Colour XYZ/LCH/HSL produce a Colour output and take Number inputs. Blend Colours interpolates between two colours using a factor, analogous to colour construction operations.

Both Blend Colours and Colour LCH produce a Colour output. Blend Colours takes Colour inputs and a Number factor, while Colour LCH takes Numbers — both are colour manipulation/creation components outputting Colour.
Both Blend Colours and Colour HSL produce a Colour output and involve numeric parameters. They are analogous colour manipulation components in the same display/colour family.

Deconstruct Material and Create Material are exact inverses sharing identical parameter sets (Kd/Ks/Ke Colours, T Number, S Integer, M Shader). They are constructor/deconstructor pairs for the same Material/Shader type.

Both Colour CMYK and Colour RGB are colour construction components that output a single Colour (C). They perform analogous operations — assembling a colour from numeric channel components — just using different colour models (CMYK vs RGB).

Colour CMYK (constructor) and Split ARGB (deconstructor) both deal with colour channel decomposition using numeric parameters (A, R, G, B / C, M, Y, K). Split ARGB is the inverse of Colour RGB, and all three are closely related colour channel components.

Colour RGB and Split ARGB are constructor/deconstructor pair for the same ARGB colour model, sharing identical channel parameters (A, R, G, B). One assembles a Colour from integer channels, the other splits a Colour into numeric channels.

Linear Dimension and Arc Dimension are both annotation/dimension components that take a Text label (T) and Scale/Size number (S) as inputs and produce a dimension display. They perform analogous dimensioning operations on different geometry types (Line vs Arc).

Make2D Parallel View and Make2D Rhino View are both view-creation components for Make2D workflows that output a View (V). They perform analogous operations — defining a projection view — using different input methods (Rectangle boundary vs named Rhino view).

Both components deal with colour channel decomposition/composition using HSV or HSL models. Colour HSV composes a Colour from A, H, S, V number inputs; Split AHSL decomposes a Colour into A, H, S, L number outputs. They are inverse operations on the same colour space parameters (alpha, hue, saturation) and share the same numeric channel types.

Both are point-based display components with no geometry outputs. Vector Display Ex takes Point (P), Colour (C), and Integer weight (W); Cloud Display takes Point (P), Colour (C), and Number size (S). Both visualize point data with colour and a size/weight parameter, producing only visual display output.

Both are annotation/dimension display components with no geometry outputs. Aligned Dimension has T (Text) and S (Number scale) inputs; Angular Dimensions (Mesh) also has T (Text), S (Number scale), and F (Number) inputs. Both produce dimension annotations as display-only output with shared text and scale parameters.

Both components produce display-only outputs (no geometry returned) and share integer/number parameters controlling visual properties (W weight in Vector Display Ex, P pattern integer and S scale in Pattern Hatch). Both also take a primary geometric input (Point+Vector vs Curve) with numeric modifiers.

Both are random number generators sharing N (count) and S (seed) integer inputs. RandomEx generates integers in a range [L0,L1], Random generates numbers within a Domain. Both use a seed for reproducibility and a count parameter.

Both involve randomness with an integer seed (S) parameter. RandomEx generates random integers, Random Reduce randomly removes items from a list using a seed. Both share the S (seed) integer input pattern.

Both Cull Nth and Cull Pattern filter/remove items from a generic list (L input → L output). They perform analogous list culling operations — one by periodic index, one by boolean pattern. Identical input/output type signatures for the list parameter.

Both Cull Nth and Cull Index remove items from a generic list (L → L). They perform analogous culling operations — one by periodic stride N, one by specific index I. Share the same list input/output pattern and list-reduction semantics.
Both Cull Pattern and Cull Index filter a generic list (L → L) and both have a boolean-type secondary parameter (P pattern / W wrap). They perform analogous list culling with a control parameter.
Both Cull Nth and Random Reduce take a generic list and produce a reduced generic list (L → L). Both perform list reduction/filtering operations, just by different criteria (periodic vs random).
Both Cull Pattern and Random Reduce take a generic list and output a filtered generic list (L → L). Both reduce list membership by different strategies (boolean mask vs random removal).
Both Cull Index and Random Reduce take a generic list and output a reduced generic list (L → L). Both remove specific items from a list by different selection strategies.

Both Duplicate Data and Stack Data take generic data (D) and produce generic data (D), both expanding/replicating data in a list. Duplicate Data repeats items N times, Stack Data stacks data S times. Analogous list-expansion operations with identical D→D signatures.

Both Series and Range generate sequences of numbers. Range takes a Domain and count N to produce evenly spaced numbers; Series takes a start, step, and count C to produce an arithmetic sequence. Both output Number sequences and share N/C integer count inputs.
Both Series and Char Sequence generate sequences — Series produces number sequences, Char Sequence produces text sequences. Both share a count parameter (C) and produce ordered sequential output.

Both Range and Random take a Domain (D/R) and an integer count N to produce N number values. Range produces evenly spaced values, Random produces randomly distributed values within the domain. Share Domain + N integer pattern.

XY Plane and YZ Plane are nearly identical: both take a single Point input (O) and output a Plane (P). They perform analogous operations constructing axis-aligned planes from an origin point, differing only in which axes define the plane.
XY Plane and XZ Plane are nearly identical: both take a single Point input (O) and output a Plane (P). They are axis-aligned plane constructors differing only in orientation.
YZ Plane and XZ Plane are nearly identical: both take a single Point input (O) and output a Plane (P). Both are axis-aligned plane constructors from an origin point.

Adjust Plane and Align Plane both take a Plane (P) and a Vector (D/N) as inputs and output a Plane (P). Both perform orientation adjustments to an existing plane using a direction vector. Align Plane also outputs an angle Number.
Adjust Plane and Align Planes both take a Plane input and output a Plane. Both perform orientation/alignment operations on planes, though Align Planes uses a reference Plane instead of a Vector.

Align Plane and Align Planes both take a Plane (P) input and output a Plane (P). Both perform alignment operations on planes relative to a direction or reference, serving analogous alignment purposes.

Plane Normal and Construct Plane both construct a Plane from a Point origin (O) and vector inputs, outputting a Plane. Plane Normal uses a single Z vector while Construct Plane uses X and Y vectors — analogous plane construction from origin + direction(s).

Plane Normal and XY Plane both construct a Plane from a Point origin (O). Plane Normal adds a Z vector for orientation while XY Plane uses a fixed orientation — both are plane constructors from an origin.

Plane Origin and Plane Offset both take a Plane input and output a Plane (Pl). Both modify an existing plane — Plane Origin repositions it to a new Point, Plane Offset shifts it along its normal by a Number. Analogous plane modification operations.

Plane Origin and Adjust Plane both take a Plane as primary input and output a Plane. Both modify an existing plane's properties (origin vs. normal direction), performing analogous plane transformation operations.

Plane 3Pt and Construct Plane both construct a Plane (Pl) from geometric inputs including Points and/or Vectors. Both are explicit plane constructors that define the plane's orientation from scratch rather than modifying an existing plane.

Deconstruct Plane and Plane Coordinates are both decomposition/analysis components that take a Plane as input and output numeric/vector components. Deconstruct Plane extracts origin and axes; Plane Coordinates extracts X/Y/Z coordinate values of a point in plane space.

Both SubD Edge Tags and SubD Vertex Tags take a SubD, a Text label, and an Integer tag value, and output a modified SubD. They perform analogous tagging operations on different SubD topology elements (edges vs vertices) with identical IO structure.

Both SubD Edges and SubD Faces are SubD decomposition/query components that take a single SubD input and output multiple descriptive data types including Text and geometry primitives. They perform analogous extraction operations on different SubD topology elements (edges vs faces).

Both SubD from Mesh and SubD Fuse convert mesh geometry into SubD output. SubD from Mesh takes one Mesh with Integer conversion parameters, while SubD Fuse takes two Meshes with Integer operation parameters. Both share the Mesh-to-SubD conversion pattern with integer control parameters.

Both MultiPipe and SubD Box are SubD geometry creation components that produce a SubD output from geometric primitives with Integer control parameters (Caps/segment counts vs division counts). Both represent direct SubD geometry generation workflows.

Both SubD Edge Tags and SubD Edges operate on SubD edges topology. SubD Edges extracts edge data including Text tags, while SubD Edge Tags sets Text tags on edges. They are complementary read/write operations on the same SubD edge topology element.

SubD Vertex Tags and SubD Faces both involve SubD vertex-level data. SubD Faces outputs vertex Text identifiers (V parameter), while SubD Vertex Tags sets Text tags on vertices. They share SubD vertex topology as a common domain.

Both take a Surface with U and V integer count inputs, both output UV point coordinates. Surface Frames outputs planes at UV grid points while Divide Surface outputs points and normals, but the grid-sampling pattern is nearly identical.

Both extract edges from a Brep and share identical output signature (Curve E, Integer I, Text M). Both filter edges based on a spatial criterion (direction vector vs. proximity to points) and share the same Brep-edge-extraction pattern.

Both extract edges from a Brep based on spatial criteria (directions vs. adjacent faces) and output Curve edges with Integer indices. All three 'Edges from X' components share the same fundamental Brep-edge-extraction operation.

Both take a Brep and a Point input to spatially filter/select edges, outputting Curve edges and Integer indices. Edges from Points uses proximity voting while Edges from Faces uses face adjacency, but the point-guided edge selection pattern is shared.

Both take two Surface inputs (S and T) and output a single Surface. Both operations transfer trimming information between surfaces — Copy Trim copies the trim curves while Retrim re-applies trimming — making them nearly identical in signature and analogous in purpose.

Both analyze Brep edges and classify/filter them, outputting integer indices identifying edge categories. Closed Edges classifies by closed/open topology while Convex Edges classifies by convexity, both performing edge-classification analysis on Breps.

Both take a Brep (or list of Breps) and output a modified Brep, performing topology-repair operations. Brep Join merges multiple Breps into closed solids while Cap Holes fills open boundary loops — both are Brep-healing/closing operations with identical input/output types.

Both take a Surface and output a modified Surface. Isotrim subsets a surface by domain while Offset Surface displaces it by distance — both are surface-transformation operations that preserve the surface type in their output.

Both take a Surface input and output a modified Surface. Both manipulate the parametric domain/orientation of the surface — Isotrim trims to a sub-domain while Reverse Surface flips U/V/W directions — analogous surface reparameterization operations.

Both take a Surface with Boolean control parameters and output a modified Surface. Both perform non-destructive surface modifications (offset vs. direction reversal) with Boolean flags controlling behavior.
Both are logarithm operations (base-10 log vs natural log) with identical x->y Generic Data signature. Analogous inverse operations of Power of 10 and Power of E respectively.
Logarithm and Power of 10 are inverse operations of each other, both using Generic Data x->y. Paired mathematical inverses.
Natural logarithm and Power of E (e^x) are inverse operations, both using identical Generic Data x->y signature.
Power of 10 and Power of 2 are analogous exponentiation operations with fixed bases, both using identical Generic Data x->y signature.
Power of 10 and Power of E are analogous fixed-base exponentiation operations, both using identical Generic Data x->y signature.
Power of 2 and Power of E are both fixed-base exponentiation operations with identical Generic Data x->y signature.
Square and Square Root are inverse operations (x^2 and x^0.5), both using identical Generic Data x->y signature.
Cube and Cube Root are inverse operations (x^3 and x^(1/3)), both using identical Generic Data x->y signature.
Square and Cube are analogous integer power operations (x^2 vs x^3), both using identical Generic Data x->y signature.
Square Root and Cube Root are analogous root extraction operations, both using identical Generic Data x->y signature.
Square and Cube Root are both power-family operations with identical Generic Data x->y signature, though not direct inverses.
Cube and Square Root are both power-family operations with identical Generic Data x->y signature.
One Over X (x^-1) and Square (x^2) are both single-input power-type operations with identical Generic Data x->y signature.
One Over X and Cube are both single-input power-type operations (x^-1 vs x^3) with identical Generic Data x->y signature.
One Over X and Square Root are both single-input power-type operations with identical Generic Data x->y signature.
Both Logarithm (base 10) and Log N (arbitrary base) perform logarithm operations. Log N generalizes Logarithm with an additional base parameter.
Both Natural Logarithm and Log N perform logarithm operations. Log N generalizes natural log with an additional base parameter.

Both rotate/orient geometry using directional vectors (From/To vectors), outputting transformed geometry and a Transform. Rotate Direction uses a single center point + from/to vectors; Orient Direction uses two point+vector pairs — analogous directional alignment operations.

Both orient geometry from one reference frame to another (Orient uses Plane A to Plane B; Orient Direction uses point+vector pairs as implicit frames). Both are orientation/alignment transforms with identical output signature.
Both map geometry from a source reference to a target reference (Orient: Plane A→B; Box Mapping: Box S→T). Structurally identical pattern of source/target remapping with same output signature.
Both map geometry from a source reference to a target reference (Orient: Plane A→B; Triangle Mapping: Curve S→T). Same structural pattern of source/target remapping with identical output signature.

Both take geometry + source (S) + target (T) references and output transformed geometry + Transform. Box Mapping uses Boxes, Triangle Mapping uses Curves, but the structural mapping pattern is identical.

Both are scaling operations outputting Geometry + Transform. Scale uses a center Point + uniform factor; Scale NU uses a Plane + three axis factors (X, Y, Z). Non-uniform scale is a direct generalization of uniform scale.

Both rotate geometry around an axis by an angle. Rotate Axis uses a Line as axis; Rotate 3D uses a Point + Vector to define the axis. Functionally equivalent rotation-around-axis operations with identical output signature.

Both are rotation transforms on geometry producing Geometry + Transform output. Rotate Axis rotates by angle around a line; Rotate Direction rotates from one vector direction to another — both are axis-based rotation operations.

Both translate/move geometry to a new position, outputting Geometry + Transform. Move uses a translation Vector; Move To Plane moves geometry onto a target Plane — both are positional displacement operations.

Both project/reflect geometry relative to a Plane, outputting Geometry + Transform. Mirror reflects across a Plane; Project Along projects onto a Plane along a direction — both are plane-based geometric projection operations.

Both use a Plane as a reference for transforming geometry and output Geometry + Transform. Shear deforms relative to a plane; Move To Plane repositions onto a plane — both are plane-referenced transforms.

Both use a Plane as primary reference input and output Geometry + Transform. Shear deforms geometry relative to a plane; Scale NU scales geometry relative to a plane — both are plane-based deformation transforms.

Both take Geometry as primary input and output Geometry + Transform. Both apply a spatial mapping/projection transformation to geometry using a reference object (Rectangle vs Point+focal length). Both are non-trivial spatial remapping operations rather than simple affine transforms.

Both take Geometry + a spatial reference (Rectangle vs Plane) and output Geometry + Transform. Both are standard geometry transformation components that apply a spatial operation and expose the underlying transform matrix.

Both take Geometry + a numeric/spatial parameter (F:Number vs A:Number angle) and output Geometry + Transform. Both perform a geometric transformation parameterized by a numeric value and a spatial reference.

Both use a Plane (P) as a key input and output a Transform (X). Both project or reorient geometry relative to a plane, and both expose the resulting transformation. Project uses Generic Data while Rotate uses typed Geometry, but the plane-based transform pattern is shared.

Both output a transformed geometry (G) and the underlying Transform (X), and both map geometry into a new coordinate space defined by a reference shape (Plane vs Rectangle pair). Both are spatial remapping operations that expose the transform for downstream reuse.

Both output transformed geometry and a Transform object. Both perform a projection-like operation (Project onto plane vs Camera Obscura perspective projection through a point), making them semantically analogous as projection transforms.

Set Intersection and Set Union are nearly identical in structure: both take two Generic Data inputs (A, B) and produce a single Generic Data output (U). They perform analogous binary set operations (intersection vs union) on the same input/output pattern.

Set Intersection and SubSet both take two Generic Data inputs (A, B) and perform set relationship operations. They differ only in output type (Generic Data vs Boolean), but conceptually both evaluate relationships between two sets.

Set Intersection and Disjoint both take two Generic Data inputs (A, B) and evaluate set relationships. Disjoint outputs a Boolean while Intersection outputs the result set, but both operate on the same binary set input pattern.
Set Union and SubSet both take two Generic Data inputs (A, B) and perform binary set operations. They share the same input pattern and operate in the same domain of set theory.
Set Union and Disjoint both take two Generic Data inputs (A, B). They are complementary set operations: union combines sets while disjoint tests if they share no members.

SubSet and Disjoint are highly similar: both take two Generic Data inputs (A, B) and output a single Boolean (R). Both are set predicate/test operations that evaluate a relationship between two sets and return true/false.
Create Set and Delete Consecutive both output Generic Data and an Integer count (M/N). Both are list/set processing operations that return a processed collection along with a count of elements.

Member Index and Delete Consecutive both output an Integer (I/N representing count or index) alongside Generic Data, and both take a set/sequence input (S). They are both set/list analysis operations that return numeric metadata about collections.

Member Index and Key/Value Search both perform lookup/search operations within a collection. Member Index finds the index of a member in a set, while Key/Value Search finds a value by key — both are search/query operations on Generic Data collections.

Both are Merge variants that take multiple Generic Data inputs (A, B, C, ...) and output a single merged stream S. Merge 10 has 10 inputs, Merge 03 has 3, but they perform identical operations with the same output parameter name S.

All three are Merge-family components that combine multiple Generic Data streams into one output. Merge (base) uses D1/D2 -> R, while Merge 10 and Merge 03 use A/B/C.../S naming, but all perform the same merge operation on Generic Data.
Both are Merge-family components combining Generic Data inputs into a single output. Merge 03 outputs S while base Merge outputs R, but both perform the same logical merge operation.

Both take a Generic Data tree T and a secondary control parameter (P for path, F for flag) and output a modified Generic Data tree T. Both are tree restructuring operations that simplify or flatten the tree structure.

Both Flatten Tree and Trim Tree take a Generic Data tree input T and produce a modified Generic Data tree output T. Both reduce tree complexity — Flatten collapses all paths, Trim removes depth levels.
Both Simplify Tree and Trim Tree take a Generic Data tree T and output a restructured Generic Data tree T. Both reduce path complexity in the data tree.
Both Simplify Tree and Match Tree take a Generic Data tree input T and output a modified Generic Data tree T. Both restructure the path topology of a data tree.
Both Flatten Tree and Match Tree take a Generic Data tree T and output a Generic Data tree T. Both modify the path structure of a data tree.

Both Flip Matrix and Explode Tree take a single Generic Data input and produce Generic Data output(s). Both perform structural transformations on data trees — Flip Matrix transposes branch/item structure, Explode Tree separates branches.

Both Shift Paths and Trim Tree take a Generic Data input D and an Integer control parameter (O for offset, D for depth) and output a modified Generic Data D. Both restructure tree paths using an integer parameter.

Both Entwine and Merge 10 take multiple Generic Data inputs and combine them into a single Generic Data output. Entwine preserves path structure while Merge flattens, but they perform analogous combination operations.

Both Entwine and Merge 03 take exactly 3 Generic Data inputs ({0;0}/{0;1}/{0;2} vs A/B/C) and produce a single Generic Data output. Both combine multiple data streams, differing in how paths are assigned.

Both Relative Items and Match Tree deal with aligning or relating two data trees (A/B inputs). Both involve tree topology matching and have wrap/guide parameters controlling how items are paired across trees.

Both Stream Gate and Shift Paths take a Generic Data input and an Integer control parameter (G for gate index, O for offset) and route/modify the data accordingly. Both use an integer to control data flow behavior.

Both Clean Tree and Graft Tree take a single Generic Data tree input (T) and output a Generic Data tree (T). They are both tree restructuring operations that transform the data tree structure without changing the underlying data types.

Both Merge Multiple and Stream Filter accept multiple Generic Data streams (inputs 0 and 1) and output a single Generic Data stream (S). They both perform stream/data combining or routing operations, and share the same multi-stream input pattern and single output pattern.

Both Clean Tree and Tree Branch take a Generic Data tree (T) as their primary input and operate on the tree structure. Both are tree inspection/manipulation operations that work on the tree as a whole unit.

Both Tree Branch and Tree Statistics take a Generic Data tree (T) as their primary input and are used to inspect or extract information from a data tree. Tree Branch extracts branch data by path, while Tree Statistics reports path/length/count metadata — both are tree-reading operations.

Both Graft Tree and Tree Branch take a Generic Data tree (T) as their primary input and produce Generic Data output. Both are fundamental tree structure operations dealing with how data is organized within branches.

Tree Statistics outputs Paths (P) and Path Compare takes a Path (P) as input — they are naturally complementary and semantically related. Both deal with tree path structures, and Tree Statistics is commonly used to feed paths into Path Compare for filtering operations.

Shortest List and Longest List are direct analogs: both take two Generic Data inputs (A, B) and produce two Generic Data outputs (A, B). They perform the same list-matching operation but with opposite truncation/extension strategies.

Shortest List and Cross Reference share identical input/output signatures (A, B → A, B with Generic Data). Both are list-matching/pairing operations that align two lists, differing only in the pairing strategy.

Longest List and Cross Reference share identical input/output signatures (A, B → A, B). Both are list-matching operations that pair two input lists, differing only in how they handle mismatched lengths.

Insert Items and Replace Items are near-identical in signature: both take L (Generic Data), I (Generic Data), i (Integer), W (Boolean) and output L (Generic Data). They perform analogous list-modification operations — inserting vs replacing elements at specified indices.

Dispatch and Split List both split a single input list into two output lists (A and B of Generic Data). Dispatch splits by Boolean pattern, Split List splits at an integer index — analogous splitting operations with the same output structure.

Dispatch and Sift Pattern both filter/split a list based on a pattern parameter and produce multiple output streams. Dispatch uses a Boolean pattern; Sift Pattern uses an Integer pattern — both perform pattern-based list partitioning.

Pick'n'Choose and Weave share identical input signatures: P (Integer), 0 (Generic Data), 1 (Generic Data). Both use an integer pattern to select/combine from two input streams. Weave interleaves items into one output; Pick'n'Choose selects items — analogous pattern-driven combination operations.

List Item and Shift List both operate on a list with an integer parameter and a wrap Boolean (W). Both use wrapping logic for index/shift behavior, making them semantically related in how they handle list traversal with wrap-around.
List Item and Insert Items both use L (list), i (Integer index), and W (Boolean wrap) parameters. Both perform index-based list access/modification with wrap-around support.

Split List and Partition List both take a list L and an integer parameter (split index vs partition size) to reorganize a list into sub-groups. Both perform list subdivision operations with an integer controlling the division.
Both are binary arithmetic operators (Power, Subtraction) with identical I/O signatures: A:Generic, B:Generic -> R:Generic
Both are binary arithmetic operators (Power, Multiplication) with identical I/O signatures: A:Generic, B:Generic -> R:Generic
Both are binary arithmetic operators (Power, Modulus) with identical I/O signatures: A:Generic, B:Generic -> R:Generic
Both are binary arithmetic operators (Subtraction, Multiplication) with identical I/O signatures: A:Generic, B:Generic -> R:Generic
Both are binary arithmetic operators (Subtraction, Modulus) with identical I/O signatures: A:Generic, B:Generic -> R:Generic
Both are binary arithmetic operators (Multiplication, Modulus) with identical I/O signatures: A:Generic, B:Generic -> R:Generic
Both are binary boolean logic gates (NAND, NOR) with identical I/O signatures: A:Boolean, B:Boolean -> R:Boolean. Both are negated forms of basic gates.
Both are numeric comparison operators (Equality, Larger Than) taking A:Number, B:Number and producing Boolean outputs. Both compare two numbers and output truth values.

Both are numeric comparison operators (Equality, Similarity) that test whether two numbers are equal (or nearly equal). Both output a Boolean equality result and take A:Number, B:Number as primary inputs.
Both are numeric comparison operators (Larger Than, Similarity) taking A:Number, B:Number and producing Boolean outputs related to numeric relationships.

Both are integer/numeric division-related operations (Integer Division, Modulus). Integer Division and Modulus are complementary operations that both divide A by B — one returns the quotient, the other the remainder.
Both are binary arithmetic operators producing a single R output from two inputs A and B. Integer Division uses Integer types specifically, Subtraction uses Generic.
Both are boolean logic gate components (Gate Majority, Gate Nand) that take Boolean inputs and produce a Boolean R output. Both operate purely in the boolean logic domain.
Both are boolean logic gate components (Gate Majority, Gate Nor) that take Boolean inputs and produce a Boolean R output.

Both Gate Or and Gate And take two Boolean inputs (A, B) and produce one Boolean output (R). They are binary logical gate operations with identical I/O signatures, differing only in the logical operation applied.

Both Gate Or and Gate Xor take two Boolean inputs (A, B) and produce one Boolean output (R). They are binary logical gate operations with identical I/O signatures, differing only in the logical operation (OR vs XOR).

Both Gate And and Gate Xor take two Boolean inputs (A, B) and produce one Boolean output (R). They are binary logical gate operations with identical I/O signatures, differing only in the logical operation (AND vs XOR).

Both Addition and Division take two Generic Data inputs (A, B) and produce one Generic Data output (R). They are binary arithmetic operations with identical I/O signatures, differing only in the arithmetic operation performed.

Both Addition and Mass Addition perform addition operations on Generic Data and produce a Generic Data result R. Mass Addition is the aggregate/list version of Addition, operating on a list of inputs rather than two explicit operands.

Gate Not and Gate Or both operate on Boolean inputs and produce Boolean output R. Gate Not is the unary version of the logical gate family, sharing the same Boolean type domain as Gate Or, And, and Xor.
Gate Not and Gate And both operate on Boolean inputs and produce Boolean output R. Gate Not is the unary logical gate, sharing the same Boolean type domain as the binary gates.
Gate Not and Gate Xor both operate on Boolean inputs and produce Boolean output R. Gate Not is the unary logical gate, sharing the same Boolean type domain as the binary gates.

Both Negative and Addition operate on Generic Data types and produce Generic Data outputs. Negative is the unary arithmetic operation analogous to the binary Addition, both working in the numeric/generic domain.
Both Negative and Division operate on Generic Data types and produce Generic Data outputs. Negative is the unary arithmetic operation in the same numeric domain as Division.
Both operate on mesh-related geometry: Simple Mesh converts Brep to Mesh, Mesh WeldVertices takes a Mesh and outputs a modified Mesh. Both are mesh processing steps in a geometry pipeline.
Both take a single Brep as input and perform a geometry processing/conversion operation on it (Simple Mesh converts Brep to Mesh; Merge Faces simplifies Brep faces).

Both operate on lists and produce reordered/filtered list outputs. Jitter randomly reorders a list (outputting Values and Indices), Sub List extracts a subrange (outputting List and Index). Both share List input and index-related outputs.
Both are list manipulation components that take a list/data input and produce a modified list/data output. Repeat Data pads a list to a given length; Sub List extracts a portion of a list.
Both are list manipulation components: Repeat Data and Jitter both accept a list and output a transformed list, operating on generic data collections.
Both are parameter/container components with no meaningful inputs or outputs in the JSON (Point and Geometry are both primitive geometry holders/parameters in Grasshopper).
Both analyze geometric properties of input geometry: Volume computes volumetric properties of geometry, Merge Faces analyzes and simplifies Brep topology. Both output multiple analytical results.

Both take a single Mesh input and produce per-face geometric data (Face Boundaries outputs curves per face, Face Normals outputs center points and normal vectors per face). Both are face-level analysis components operating on the same mesh topology.

Both take a single Mesh input and output Point and Vector data. Deconstruct Mesh outputs vertices (Point) and normals (Vector); Face Normals outputs face centers (Point) and face normals (Vector). Both decompose mesh geometry into positional and directional components.

Both take a single Mesh input and analyze mesh edge topology. Mesh Edges outputs categorized edge lines (naked, interior, non-manifold); Mesh NakedEdge outputs naked edge vertex indices and connectivity. Both are edge-level mesh analysis tools focused on boundary/topology classification.

Both take a single Mesh input and extract boundary-related geometric information. Mesh Edges outputs edge lines including naked edges; Face Boundaries outputs boundary curves per face. Both reveal the geometric boundary structure of a mesh.

Both take Mesh as primary input and produce face-level mesh data. Deconstruct Mesh outputs Mesh face data; Mesh Explode separates mesh into individual face meshes. Both decompose a mesh into its constituent face elements.

Both take a Mesh input and output Boolean values used for filtering or testing. Mesh Inclusion tests if points are inside a mesh (Boolean output); Mesh Depth filters mesh vertices by depth range (Boolean validity output). Both produce Boolean masks derived from mesh spatial queries.

Both take a single Mesh input and extract structured data from it. Mesh ExtractAttributes pulls attribute data (text keys and generic values); Deconstruct Mesh extracts geometric components (vertices, faces, colors, normals). Both are mesh decomposition/extraction components.

Deconstruct Matrix and Construct Matrix are exact inverses sharing the same parameter set (R: Integer, C: Integer, V: Number, M: Matrix). They are a perfect construct/deconstruct pair operating on the same data types.

Swap Columns and Swap Rows are nearly identical operations: both take a Matrix M and two Integer indices (A, B) and output a Matrix M. They perform the same swap operation but on different axes (columns vs rows), making them highly analogous.
Both Deconstruct Matrix and Transpose Matrix take a single Matrix as input and produce outputs derived from that matrix. Both are single-input matrix analysis/transformation operations.
Swap Columns and Transpose Matrix both take a Matrix as input and output a Matrix. Both are in-place matrix transformation operations that rearrange the structure of the matrix.
Swap Rows and Transpose Matrix both take a Matrix as input and output a Matrix. Both are structural matrix transformation operations that modify how matrix elements are arranged.

Identical input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number) and identical output type (P: Generic Data). Both are Kangaroo2 mesh-based goal components that produce a goal object from a mesh and strength value.
Identical input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number) and identical output type (P: Generic Data). Both are Kangaroo2 mesh smoothing/pressure goal components with the same parameter structure.
Identical input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number) and identical output type (P: Generic Data). TangentialSmooth and Smooth are both mesh smoothing goals sharing the same IO pattern.

Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). Both are Kangaroo2 mesh goal components; only output name differs (P vs G). Isothermic and Pressure both operate on mesh geometry with a strength parameter.
Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). Both are Kangaroo2 mesh goal components operating on mesh geometry with a strength parameter.
Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). Both are Kangaroo2 mesh goal components; Pressure and Developablize both take a mesh and strength and output a goal object.
Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). TangentialSmooth and Isothermic are both mesh-based Kangaroo2 goals with identical input structure.
Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). TangentialSmooth and Conicalize are both mesh-based Kangaroo2 goals with identical input structure.
Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). TangentialSmooth and Developablize are both mesh-based Kangaroo2 goals with identical input structure.
Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). Isothermic and Smooth are both mesh-based Kangaroo2 goals with identical input structure.
Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). Isothermic and Conicalize are both mesh-based Kangaroo2 goals with identical input structure.
Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). Isothermic and Developablize are both mesh-based Kangaroo2 goals with identical input structure.
Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). Conicalize and Smooth are both mesh-based Kangaroo2 goals with identical input structure.
Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). Conicalize and Developablize are both mesh-based Kangaroo2 goals with identical input structure.
Same input signature (M: Mesh, Strength: Number). Smooth and Developablize are both mesh-based Kangaroo2 goals with identical input structure.

Both PlasticHinge and NoFoldThrough take FoldStart, FoldEnd, Tip1, Tip2 (Points) and Strength (Number) as inputs, and output H (Generic Data). They model fold constraints in Kangaroo2 with nearly identical IO structure; PlasticHinge adds RestAngle and Limit parameters.

Both EdgeLengths and VertexLoads take a Mesh and Strength (Number) as inputs and output a Generic Data goal. They share the mesh+strength pattern and are both Kangaroo2 mesh-based load/constraint goals.
Both EdgeLengths and Pressure take a Mesh and Strength as inputs and output Generic Data. EdgeLengths adds LengthFactor but the core pattern is the same Kangaroo2 mesh goal structure.

Both Volume and Pressure take a Mesh (M) and Strength (Number) as core inputs and output Generic Data. Volume adds a target volume parameter V but shares the fundamental mesh+strength Kangaroo2 goal pattern.

Both TangentIncircles and Pressure take a Mesh (M) and Strength (Number) as core inputs and output Generic Data. TangentIncircles adds a Curve boundary parameter but shares the fundamental mesh+strength Kangaroo2 goal pattern.

Both take a Curve and a parameter t (Number) as inputs. Evaluate Curve outputs Point, Vector, Angle while Curve Frame outputs a Plane — both sample a curve at parameter t to get geometric frame/position data. Nearly identical input signatures and analogous evaluation operations.

Both take Curve and Number (t) as inputs, performing parameter-based evaluation along a curve. Length Parameter queries arc-length distances at a given parameter, analogous to curve frame evaluation at a parameter.

Both accept Curve + Number (t parameter) inputs and evaluate curve properties at that parameter. Evaluate Curve returns positional/tangent data; Length Parameter returns length measurements — both are point-in-parameter-space queries.

Both take a single Curve input and output Boolean values describing geometric properties of the curve (Planar outputs planarity boolean + plane; Closed outputs closed/periodic booleans). Both are curve property testers with Boolean outputs.

Both take a single Curve as input and analyze intrinsic curve properties. Planar checks planarity and returns a plane; Control Polygon extracts the underlying control structure. Both are single-curve analysis components with no additional parameters.
Both accept a single Curve input and extract intrinsic structural information (Closed checks topology; Control Polygon extracts control points). Single-curve, no-parameter analysis components.
Both output Points derived from a Curve. End Points extracts start/end points; Evaluate Curve outputs a point at parameter t. Both are point-extraction operations on curves.

Both extract Points from a Curve and also output Number/parameter values (t). End Points gives start/end; Discontinuity gives special parameter points. Both are point-extraction components from curve geometry.

Both involve spatial relationship queries between points/curves. Curve Proximity finds closest points between two curves (outputs Points + distance); Point in Curves tests containment of a point relative to curves (outputs point + relationship integers). Both output Points and involve curve-point spatial analysis.

Both take a single Curve (polygon/planar curve) input and compute geometric center/plane information. Polygon Center finds centroid variants; Planar finds the plane of the curve. Both analyze planar curve geometry to extract center/plane data.

Both compute length-related Number outputs from a Curve. Length Domain computes length over a Domain sub-interval; Length Parameter computes arc-length distances at a parameter. Both are arc-length measurement components on curves outputting Numbers.

Both output Points and Numbers from Curve inputs. Discontinuity outputs Points and t parameters; Evaluate Curve outputs Point, Vector, and angle Number. Both sample/extract point and parameter data from curves.

Both take a Curve and a Number as inputs and output positional/geometric data (Plane vs Point+Vector). Both evaluate a curve at a parameter or length position, performing analogous curve evaluation operations.

Both perform proximity/closest-point queries involving a curve. Curve Closest Point finds the closest point on a curve from a given point; Curve Nearest Object finds the closest geometry to a curve. Both output Point(s) and an index/distance Number, representing analogous nearest-neighbor operations.
Both take a Curve input and output a curve parameter value (t: Number), enabling downstream parameter-based curve evaluation. Both are used to extract parametric information from a curve.

Both output a Point (P), a curve parameter (t: Number), and take a Curve input. Both resolve a location on a curve — one from a length, the other from a closest-point query — producing the same set of output types (Point, parameter t).
Both are light source components with a Light typed input/output and a positional parameter (Point). Both follow the same get/set pattern for light objects.
Both are light source components with a Light typed input/output and a geometry parameter defining the light's position/shape. Both follow the same get/set pattern.
Both are light source components sharing a Light typed input/output. Both define a spatial light with geometric parameters (Point/Vector vs Plane/dimensions).
Both are simple light source components (Point Light vs Linear Light) with a Light typed input/output and a single geometry input defining position/shape.
Both are positional light source components with Light typed input/output. Point Light uses a Point while Rectangular Light uses a Plane with dimensions.
Both are extended light source components (Linear Light vs Rectangular Light) with Light typed input/output and geometry inputs defining the light shape.
Both are Query components that take a Text Pattern input (N) and return model content objects (Model Environment vs Model Texture). Identical structural pattern of querying model assets by name.
Both Sun and Skylight are render settings components sharing Model Content and Boolean typed inputs/outputs. Both control scene-level lighting with enable/disable Boolean flags.
Both relate to render options/settings. Query Render Options outputs Model Content (S) which is the same type as Sun's Model Content output, suggesting Sun settings are part of render options.
Skylight outputs Model Content (Sk) which matches the Sk output of Query Render Options. Both deal with skylight/environment render settings.

Offset Curve Loose and Offset Curve are nearly identical: both take a curve, a distance number, and a plane, and both output a curve. They perform the same operation (offsetting) but with different algorithms (loose vs. exact).
Rebuild Curve and Fit Curve both take a curve and an integer degree parameter and output a curve. Both refit/reconstruct a curve to a new NURBS representation with a specified degree.
Simplify Curve and Reduce both take a curve and a tolerance/threshold number and output a simplified/reduced curve. Both aim to reduce curve complexity within a tolerance.
Simplify Curve and Curve To Polyline both take a curve with tolerance parameters and output a simplified curve representation. Both reduce geometric complexity using tolerance thresholds.
Fillet Distance and Seam both take a Curve and a Number and output a Curve. Both modify a closed/open curve at a parameter or distance along it.

Pull Curve and Project Curve both map a curve onto a surface/brep geometry and output a curve. Both perform curve-to-surface projection operations, differing only in method (pull vs. directional project).
Rebuild Curve and Reduce both take a curve and integer parameters and output a curve. Both restructure the underlying point/segment representation of a curve.

Smooth Polyline and Reduce both operate on polyline curves and output modified polylines. Both take an integer parameter controlling the degree of modification and simplify or smooth the polyline geometry.
Curve To Polyline and Reduce both output a curve plus an integer (segment count / reduction count), and both take a curve with numeric tolerance inputs to control the simplification process.

Both components take a Curve as primary input and output a Curve. They belong to the same curve_utilities family and operate as curve modification/transformation tools. Fillet modifies curve geometry while Flip Curve changes curve direction, both producing a transformed curve as output.

Both take a Mesh input and produce two Mesh outputs (R0/R1 and T/F), both partition mesh faces into two groups — one by integer index, one by boolean pattern. Analogous face-rerouting operations with dual-output structure.

Both extract geometric primitives from a mesh: Mesh Edges extracts Lines (edges) and Face Polylines extracts Curves (face boundaries). Both are mesh-to-curve-like extraction operations with a single geometry input and a single curve/line output.

Both take Geometry as input and extract geometric sub-elements: Mesh Edges extracts Lines, Vertices Component extracts Points. Both are mesh decomposition/extraction components with a single geometry input.

Both take Geometry as input and extract boundary/topological elements: Vertices Component extracts Points, Naked Boundary extracts Curves. Both are single-input extraction components operating on mesh geometry.

Both take mesh/geometry input and produce a single cleaned/unified mesh/geometry output. Both are mesh processing/repair operations: Unify Face Windings fixes normals, Join Meshes and Weld merges and welds meshes. Analogous mesh cleanup operations.

Both take a mesh-like input and output Curves: Face Polylines outputs face boundary polylines, Naked Boundary outputs boundary curves of naked edges. Both extract curve representations from mesh topology.
Both Number and Integer are numeric primitive parameter containers with identical empty I/O structure, differing only in numeric type (float vs int)
Number and Constant are both numeric value holders with no I/O; Constant typically holds fixed numeric values similar to Number parameter
Integer and Constant both hold fixed numeric values with identical empty I/O structure
Text and Data Path are both string/text-based parameter containers; Data Path is essentially a structured text path, sharing the same empty I/O pattern and string semantics
Text and Culture both deal with string/locale representations and share identical empty I/O structure
Data and Data Path are both generic data container parameters with identical empty I/O structure, both dealing with abstract data organization
Data and Marshalling signal parameter both serve as generic data transport/container mechanisms with identical empty I/O structure
Complex and Number are both numeric parameter types with empty I/O; Complex numbers extend real numbers, making them semantically related numeric primitives
Time and Unit System are both system-level metadata parameters (temporal and spatial measurement systems) with identical empty I/O structure
Hyper Index and Data Path both represent structured addressing/indexing schemes for data trees with identical empty I/O structure
Font and Colour are both display/rendering property parameters used for visual styling, sharing identical empty I/O structure
Colour and Shader are both visual/rendering parameters used to define appearance of geometry, sharing identical empty I/O structure and display semantics

Both are Domain parameter components (Domain and Domain²), representing interval/range primitives. Domain² is the 2D extension of Domain, sharing the same conceptual purpose of defining numeric intervals. Both are primitive parameter holders with no inputs.

Both divide a domain into sub-domains using integer count(s). Divide Domain takes a 1D Domain and count C, outputs Domain segments. Divide Domain² takes a 2D Domain² and U/V counts, outputs Domain² segments. Analogous operations differing only in dimensionality.

Both deconstruct a domain type into its numeric boundary components. Deconstruct Domain takes Domain→(S,E numbers), Deconstruct Domain² takes Domain²→(U0,U1,V0,V1 numbers). Same pattern of decomposing domain into constituent number values, differing only in 1D vs 2D.

Both construct a domain from simpler components. Construct Domain takes two Numbers (A,B) and outputs a 1D Domain. Construct Domain² takes two Domains (U,V) and outputs a 2D Domain². Analogous construction pattern where the 2D version uses 1D domains as inputs instead of numbers.

Deconstruct Domain and Construct Domain are inverse operations on the same Domain type. Deconstruct Domain: Domain→(Number,Number); Construct Domain: (Number,Number)→Domain. They share the same parameter types and are semantically paired as construct/deconstruct inverses.

Deconstruct Domain² and Construct Domain² are inverse operations on the Domain² type. Deconstruct Domain²: Domain²→Numbers; Construct Domain²: (Domain,Domain)→Domain². Semantically paired as the 2D equivalents of the construct/deconstruct pair.

Both produce Domain outputs from numeric inputs. Divide Domain takes a Domain and Integer count to produce sub-Domains. Consecutive Domains takes Numbers and a Boolean to produce sequential Domains. Both generate Domain collections from numeric parameters.

Both take numeric inputs and produce a Domain output. Bounds takes a list of Numbers and outputs the bounding Domain. Construct Domain takes two Numbers (A,B) and outputs a Domain. Both are domain-creation components from numeric data.

Both create Domain outputs from Number inputs. Bounds computes the numeric range of a set of numbers as a Domain. Consecutive Domains creates sequential Domains from size Numbers. Both serve as domain-generation utilities from numeric data.

Both operate on Domain inputs together with Number inputs to produce numeric outputs. Remap Numbers maps a Number value between Domain ranges. Find Domain locates which Domain in a collection contains a Number. Both relate numbers to domains with similar input signatures.

Both create closed conic curves (Circle vs Ellipse). Circle CNR takes center point + normal + radius; Ellipse takes plane + two radii. Both output a curve (Circle/Ellipse). Analogous shape-creation operations with radius parameters.

Both create closed planar curves centered at a point/plane with a radius parameter. Circle CNR uses center+normal+radius; Polygon uses plane+radius+sides. Both output a closed curve and share the radius Number input.

Both output a Circle. Circle CNR constructs from center/normal/radius; Circle TanTan constructs from tangent curves and a point. Analogous circle-creation operations with different construction methods.

Both create a Line and output it as type Line. Line takes two Points (A, B); Line SDL takes a start Point, direction Vector, and length Number. Analogous line-creation operations — both produce a Line from point-based inputs.

Both involve Line geometry as output (type Line). Line creates from two points; Line 2Plane trims/extends a line between two planes. Both are line-construction/manipulation operations outputting a Line.
Both take Point inputs and output a Line. Line uses exactly two points; Fit Line fits a best-fit line through a collection of points. Analogous line-from-points operations.
Both output a Line. Line SDL constructs a line from start point, direction, and length; Line 2Plane modifies an existing line relative to planes. Both produce Line geometry.

Both create Rectangle geometry and output both a Rectangle (R) and a Number (L, likely perimeter/length). Rectangle 3Pt uses three points; Rectangle uses a plane and X/Y domains. Analogous rectangle-creation operations sharing the same output signature.

Both take a Plane (P) and Number radius input(s) and output a closed curve plus a Number (L, likely perimeter). Ellipse outputs curve+foci; Polygon outputs curve+side length. Both are plane-based closed curve constructors.

Both create an Ellipse curve. InEllipse fits an ellipse through three points and outputs the ellipse curve + plane; Ellipse constructs from plane + two radii and outputs ellipse curve + focal points. Directly analogous ellipse-creation operations.
Both take exactly three Point inputs (A, B, C) and output a curve. InEllipse outputs an inscribed ellipse; Rectangle 3Pt outputs a rectangle. Analogous 3-point curve construction operations.

Both output a Curve and take an Integer parameter (K = degree/knot style for Interpolate(t); C = continuity for Blend Curve). Both are spline/curve construction operations with a curve output and an integer control parameter.
Both take Curve inputs and output Curve(s). Blend Curve blends between two curves; Iso Curve extracts curves from a surface. Both are curve-derivation operations.

Both take three Points (A, B, C) and output Circle, Plane, and Number R. Circle 3Pt finds the circumscribed circle; InCircle finds the inscribed circle — analogous geometric constructions with identical I/O signatures.

Both take three Points (A, B, C) and output a Plane and Number R. Arc 3Pt outputs Geometry (Arc) while Circle 3Pt outputs Circle — both fit a circle/arc through three points with nearly identical input pattern.
Both InCircle and Arc 3Pt take three Points and output Plane and Number R. They differ only in the primary output type (Circle vs Arc/Geometry) but share the three-point construction pattern.

Both Nurbs Curve and Kinky Curve take Point list V and Integer degree D, and output Curve, Number (length), and Domain. They both construct curves from point lists with a degree parameter — Nurbs Curve uses a periodicity boolean while Kinky Curve uses an angle threshold.

Nurbs Curve and Interpolate share identical inputs (V: Point, D: Integer, P: Boolean) and identical outputs (C: Curve, L: Number, D: Domain). Both construct curves from point lists with degree and periodicity. Interpolate adds a knot style parameter K.

Kinky Curve and Interpolate both take Point list V and Integer D, outputting Curve, Number, and Domain. Both are point-list-to-curve constructors with a degree parameter; they differ in the third input (angle threshold vs periodicity+knot style).

PolyLine and PolyArc both take a list of Points (V) and a Boolean closure flag (C), outputting a single Curve. Both construct piecewise curves from point sequences with optional closing — PolyArc adds tangent vectors T for arc fitting.

Arc and Modified Arc both involve Arc construction with a radius (R: Number) input and output an Arc. Arc uses Plane + Domain while Modified Arc modifies an existing arc via Domain and R — both are arc-construction/modification tools sharing the R and Arc output.
Arc and Swing Arc both take a Plane (P) and Number (R) as inputs and produce arc/circle geometry. Both are arc-family constructors operating in a plane with a radius parameter.

BiArc and Arc both output Arc geometry (BiArc outputs two arcs A1, A2) and both accept a Number R parameter. Both are arc-construction components — BiArc fits two tangent arcs between points while Arc constructs a single arc from plane/radius/domain.

Curve On Surface and Nurbs Curve share the same output signature (C: Curve, L: Number, D: Domain) and both have a Boolean closure/closed parameter. Both produce curves with length and domain information.
Curve On Surface and Kinky Curve share identical output signatures (C: Curve, L: Number, D: Domain). Both produce parameterized curves with length and domain outputs.

Catenary and PolyLine both take Point inputs and output a single Curve. Both construct a curve connecting points — Catenary uses physics-based hanging chain geometry between two points while PolyLine connects multiple points with straight segments.

Both Match Curve and Blend Curve Pt take two Curve inputs (A, B) and an Integer continuity parameter (C), outputting a Curve. Both perform curve blending/matching operations with continuity control via integer enum.
Both Match Curve and Tween Curve take two Curve inputs (A, B) and output a single Curve. Both perform interpolation/transition operations between two curves.
Both Blend Curve Pt and Tween Curve take two Curve inputs (A, B) and output a Curve. Both create transitional curves between two input curves.
Both Nurbs Curve PWK and Bezier Span output a Curve (C), a Length number (L), and a Domain (D). Both are low-level curve construction components that provide full curve metadata on output.

Both Circle and Arc SED are primitive conic curve constructors. Arc SED outputs a radius (R) and plane (P) analogous to Circle's inputs, and both deal with circular geometry. They are analogous operations (full circle vs arc segment).
Both Catenary Ex and Tween Curve take A and B endpoint/curve inputs and output Curve(s). Both create interpolated or physically-derived curves between two defined positions.

Both Match Curve and Connect Curves take Curve input(s) and an Integer parameter controlling continuity/grade (G vs C integer), outputting a Curve. Both manipulate curve connectivity with continuity control.

Both Mesh Extrude and Mesh Offset take a Mesh input along with Solid? and Both Sides? boolean flags, and both output a Mesh. They perform analogous mesh thickening/extension operations with identical boolean control parameters, differing only in the primary operation parameter (Dir vector vs Offset number).
Both Mesh Extrude and Mesh Reduce take a Mesh as input and output a modified Mesh. Both are mesh transformation operations, though they serve different purposes (extrusion vs. polygon reduction).
Both Mesh Offset and Mesh Reduce take a Mesh as input and output a modified Mesh. Both are mesh modification operations that alter geometry while preserving mesh topology structure.
Both take a Mesh as primary input and belong to the same LunchBox mesh family, though Mesh Edges outputs edge curves rather than a modified mesh.
Both take a Mesh as primary input and belong to the same LunchBox mesh family, though their operations and outputs differ significantly.

Both Mesh Reduce and Mesh Edges take a Mesh as primary input and include a numeric secondary parameter (Accuracy/Angle). Both are analytical/processing operations on mesh geometry within the same LunchBox family.

Both are solid boolean operations on two Brep inputs producing a Brep output. Solid Intersection and Solid Difference are analogous operations in the same boolean family, differing only in the boolean logic applied.

Both are solid boolean operations on Brep geometry producing Brep output. Solid Union and Solid Intersection are the classic Boolean pair; Union takes a single list while Intersection takes two explicit inputs but both operate in the same domain.
Both are solid boolean operations (Difference and Union) on Brep geometry producing Brep output, forming the core solid boolean triad together with Intersection.

Both are mesh boolean operations taking two Mesh inputs (A, B) and producing a Mesh output (R). Mesh Intersection and Mesh Difference are analogous mesh-domain counterparts to the solid boolean operations.
Both operate on Mesh geometry and produce Mesh output, forming the mesh boolean triad. Mesh Union and Mesh Intersection share the same domain and output type.
Both operate on Mesh geometry and produce Mesh output. Mesh Difference and Mesh Union are complementary boolean operations in the mesh domain.

Both are planar region boolean operations taking Curve inputs and a Plane (P) and producing Curve output (R). Region Intersection and Region Union are analogous 2D curve-domain boolean operations with identical I/O structure.

Both Split Brep and Split Brep Multiple take a Brep (B) and a cutting Brep (C) and produce Brep output (R). They perform the same splitting operation; Multiple is the multi-cutter variant of Split Brep.
Both Split Brep and Trim Solid operate on Brep geometry with a second Brep as a cutting/trimming tool and produce Brep output. They are analogous cutting operations on solid geometry.
Both Split Brep Multiple and Trim Solid use a Brep as cutter against another Brep and produce Brep output, performing analogous cutting/trimming operations on solid geometry.
Both take two Brep inputs and produce Brep output. Solid Intersection and Split Brep both operate on pairs of Breps to produce modified Brep geometry, sharing the same fundamental I/O pattern.

Both Box Slits and Region Slits are slit-generating operations that take a gap/geometry parameter (G as Number) and produce an integer type output (T). They are analogous slitting operations in 3D (box) and 2D (region) domains respectively.

Mesh Intersection and Solid Intersection are domain-equivalent operations (intersection boolean) applied to different geometry types (Mesh vs Brep), sharing the same semantic operation and A/B input pattern.

Mesh Difference and Solid Difference are domain-equivalent operations (difference boolean) applied to different geometry types (Mesh vs Brep), sharing the same semantic operation and A/B input naming pattern.

Mesh Union and Solid Union are domain-equivalent operations (union boolean) applied to different geometry types (Mesh vs Brep), both taking a single collection input and producing unified geometry output.

IronPython 2 Script and Python 3 Script are nearly identical: both take x (Generic Data), y (Generic Data) as inputs and output out (Text) and a (Generic Data). They perform the same scripting role but target different Python runtimes.

IronPython 2 Script and DotNET C# Script (LEGACY) share identical input/output structure: x, y Generic Data inputs and out (Text) + A/a (Generic Data) outputs. Both are scripting components that allow custom code execution with the same default parameter pattern.

Python 3 Script and DotNET C# Script (LEGACY) share identical input/output structure: x, y Generic Data inputs and out (Text) + A/a (Generic Data) outputs. Both are general-purpose scripting components differing only in language.

VB Script and IronPython 2 Script share the same default I/O pattern (x, y Generic Data in; out Text, A/a Generic Data out). Both are legacy scripting components with analogous roles in GH, differing only in language.
VB Script and Python 3 Script share identical default I/O structure. Both are scripting components accepting generic inputs x, y and producing a text log output and a generic data result.
VB Script and DotNET C# Script (LEGACY) share the same default I/O pattern and are both legacy .NET-based scripting components in Grasshopper, performing analogous custom code execution roles.

Expression and Evaluate components both operate on mathematical expressions with x and y Expression Variant inputs and return a Generic Data result R. Evaluate adds an explicit Expression input E, but both perform expression evaluation with the same core I/O pattern and purpose.

var and Variable components both have no inputs or outputs defined and serve as variable/parameter placeholder components in the scripting context, suggesting they perform analogous roles as named data holders or pass-through references.
Both are 1D geometric primitives (Line and Circular Arc) with no inputs/outputs in param form; both represent curve-like geometry types used as primitive inputs in GH workflows
Both are vector-type parameters (Vector and MetaVector); analogous geometric direction/magnitude containers used similarly in vector field and force workflows
Both are polygon mesh-like geometry parameters (Mesh and SubD); analogous discrete surface representations used interchangeably in mesh processing workflows
Both represent mesh data structures (Mesh and PlanktonMesh); PlanktonMesh is a half-edge mesh variant analogous to the standard GH Mesh parameter
