SubD and PlanktonMesh are both advanced mesh-like representations beyond standard Mesh; both support topological operations and subdivision-style workflows
Both are annotation/dimension geometry parameters (Leader and Angular Dimension); both represent annotation objects in Rhino/GH documentation workflows
Both are abstract non-geometric data containers (View and Field) with no direct geometric primitive; both wrap complex Rhino-side objects passed as opaque params
Line and Vector are closely related geometric primitives; both encode direction and magnitude in 3D space and are often used interchangeably in direction-based operations
Point Cloud and Mesh are both discrete point-based geometry representations; Point Cloud is an unstructured set of points analogous to mesh vertices without connectivity
Transform and Twisted Box both encode spatial transformation information; Twisted Box defines a local coordinate frame deformation analogous to a spatial transform container
Both are geometry parameter containers (Brep and Curve) with no inputs and direct geometry output, serving as primary geometric data holders in Grasshopper
Both are fundamental geometry parameter types (Brep and Plane) with identical structure: no inputs, direct geometry output
Both are core geometric parameter holders (Curve and Plane) used as inputs to geometric operations, same structural pattern
Both are annotation/dimension parameter types (Centermark and Radial Dimension) used in technical drawing contexts, sharing the same annotation domain
Both are annotation-related parameter containers (Centermark and Text Entity) used in drafting/documentation workflows
Both are annotation parameter types (Centermark and Annotation Dot) used for marking and labeling in technical drawings
Both are annotation parameter containers (Radial Dimension and Text Entity) used in technical documentation contexts
Both are annotation parameter types (Radial Dimension and Annotation Dot) for marking geometry in drawings
Both are text-based annotation parameters (Text Entity and Annotation Dot) that display textual information attached to geometry
Both are Rhino object reference parameters (Location and Block Instance) that reference positioned/placed objects in the Rhino document
Both are Rhino scene object parameters (Light and Location) that reference non-geometry scene elements with positional properties

Both Rectangular Array and Box Array take a Geometry input plus integer count parameters (X, Y for rectangular; X, Y, Z for box) and a spatial container (Rectangle vs Box). Both output Geometry and Transform. Box Array is essentially the 3D extension of Rectangular Array.
Both Rectangular Array and Linear Array produce evenly spaced copies of geometry along a defined direction/region, share Geometry in/out and Transform output, and both use integer count parameters.

Both Curve Array and Linear Array share identical parameter signatures (G: Geometry, N: Integer, path/direction input) and identical outputs (G: Geometry, X: Transform). Both distribute geometry N times along a path — one along a curve, one along a vector direction.

Both Curve Array and Polar Array use N as the count of copies, take a path/reference (Curve vs Plane+Angle) to define distribution, and produce identical outputs (Geometry + Transform). Both distribute geometry evenly along a defined locus.

Both Linear Array and Polar Array share the same parameter pattern (G: Geometry, N: Integer, direction/plane input) and identical outputs (G: Geometry, X: Transform). Linear distributes along a vector; Polar distributes around a plane — analogous 1D array operations in different coordinate systems.

Both Rectangular Array and Curve Array distribute geometry copies and output Geometry + Transform. Rectangular uses a Rectangle container with X/Y counts; Curve uses a Curve path with N count — both are path-based array operations with similar output semantics.

Box Array and Linear Array both produce spatial arrays of geometry with integer count controls and share identical output types (Geometry + Transform). Box Array extends the linear concept into 3D grid space.

Box Array and Polar Array both distribute geometry in a volumetric/angular space with integer count parameters and share identical output types (Geometry + Transform). Both define array extents via a spatial reference (Box vs Plane+Angle).

BouncySolver and Solver are nearly identical: same input/output structure (GoalObjects, Reset, Threshold, Tolerance, On → I, V, O), same purpose as iterative physics solvers. BouncySolver adds Damping and Iterations parameters, making it a superset of Solver.

BouncySolver and ZombieSolver share the core solver I/O pattern (GoalObjects, Threshold, Tolerance → I, V, O). ZombieSolver is a non-interactive batch solver variant, analogous to BouncySolver but without Reset/On controls and with a MaxIterations cap.

Solver and ZombieSolver share identical output structure (I, V, O) and core inputs (GoalObjects, Threshold, Tolerance). Both solve Kangaroo physics goals; ZombieSolver is the headless/batch variant of Solver without interactive Reset/On controls.

BouncySolver and Soft & Hard Solver share the same interactive solver outputs (I, V, O) and control inputs (Reset, Threshold, Tolerance, On). Soft & Hard Solver extends the concept by splitting goals into soft and hard categories with separate iteration control.

Solver and Soft & Hard Solver share identical outputs (I, V, O) and interactive control inputs (Reset, Threshold, Tolerance, On). Soft & Hard Solver is an extended variant that separates goals into soft/hard categories, analogous to the standard Solver.

ZombieSolver and Soft & Hard Solver both share the core solver outputs (I, V, O) and convergence inputs (Threshold, Tolerance). Both extend the basic Solver concept in different directions: ZombieSolver for batch processing, Soft & Hard Solver for goal prioritization.

Inverse operations: Serialize Geometry converts Geo→Text while Deserialize Geometry converts Text→Geo. They share the same data types (Generic Data / Text) and are complementary serialization/deserialization operations on geometry.
Both operate on geometry/generic data and produce a transformed text/data representation. Both are read-only transformations that encode object information into another format.

Both take Generic Data as input and produce Generic Data as output. Both encode object information into a derived representation (serialized text vs hash), and both are non-destructive transformations.
Both take Text as a primary input and produce Generic Data as output. Both are decoding/deserialization-type operations that transform encoded text into usable data.
Both take two Time inputs (A and B) and produce a Time output. Both operate on a range/interpolation between two date/time values, making them analogous operations on the same data type.

Both construct a Time output from Integer inputs representing time components (hours, minutes, seconds). Construct Date uses Y/M/D/h/m/s integers while Construct Time uses H/M/S integers — analogous construction operations from numeric parts to a Time value.
Both take multiple Time inputs and produce a single Time output. Combine Date & Time merges two Time values while Interpolate Date blends two Time values — both are binary Time→Time operations.
Both accept Time inputs (D/T vs A/B) and produce a Time output R. Both combine or relate multiple Time values into a resulting Time value.
Nearly identical components: both 'Split with Brep(s)' take Curve+Brep inputs and output Curve+Point. Singular vs plural variant performing the same operation.
Nearly identical components: both 'Trim with Brep(s)' take Curve+Brep inputs and output Ci+Co (inside/outside curves). Singular vs plural variant performing the same operation.
Nearly identical components: both 'Trim with Region(s)' take Curve+Curve(region)+Plane inputs and output Ci+Co. Singular vs plural variant performing the same operation.
Both are trim operations outputting inside/outside curve segments (Ci, Co). Differ in trimming boundary type: Brep vs planar region curve.
Both are trim operations outputting inside/outside curve segments (Ci, Co). Differ in trimming boundary type: Brep vs planar region curve.
Both are trim operations outputting inside/outside curve segments (Ci, Co). Differ in trimming boundary type: Brep vs planar region curve.
Both are trim operations outputting inside/outside curve segments (Ci, Co). Differ in trimming boundary type: Brep vs planar region curve.
Both split/trim a curve using a Brep boundary. Split outputs segments+points; Trim outputs inside/outside classification. Analogous curve-brep intersection operations.
Both split/trim a curve using a Brep boundary. Split outputs segments+points; Trim outputs inside/outside classification. Analogous curve-brep intersection operations.
Both operate on Curve+Brep inputs to produce curve results. Split with Breps outputs raw segments; Trim with Breps classifies inside/outside.
Both operate on Curve+Brep inputs to produce curve results. Split with Breps outputs raw segments; Trim with Brep classifies inside/outside.

Both are key-value filter components with identical input signatures (K: Text, V: Generic Data) and both output Predicate types. Equality Filter outputs =,≠ predicates while Greater Than Filter outputs >,≥ predicates — analogous comparison operations on the same data pattern.

Both are key-value filter components with identical input signatures (K: Text, V: Generic Data) and both output Predicate types. Equality Filter outputs =,≠ predicates while Less Than Filter outputs <,≤ predicates — analogous comparison operations.

Greater Than Filter and Less Than Filter are near-identical in structure: same inputs (K: Text, V: Generic Data), same output types (two Predicates representing strict and non-strict variants). They are inverse/complementary comparison filter operations.

Both Intersection Filter and Logical And Filter take Predicate inputs and output a single Predicate. They both combine multiple predicates into one, performing logical aggregation (AND/intersection semantics are effectively equivalent for set-based filtering).

Intersection Filter and Union Filter share identical I/O signatures (F: Predicate → F: Predicate). Both are predicate combinators that aggregate multiple filters into one, differing only in the logical operation (AND/intersection vs OR/union).
Logical And Filter and Union Filter both take Predicate inputs and output a single combined Predicate. They are complementary logical combinators (AND vs OR) with the same structural signature.

Group Content and Order Content have identical input signatures (C: Model Content, K: Text) and identical output signatures (C: Model Content, V: Generic Data). Both operate on model content collections using a key, differing only in their operation (grouping vs ordering).

Group Content and User Text both take Model Content and a Text key as inputs and output Model Content. Both are content-manipulation components that annotate or organize model content using key-based metadata.
Order Content and User Text both accept Model Content + Text key inputs and output Model Content. Both manipulate model content using text-based keys for metadata operations.

Duplicate Content and Content Cache both take Model Content as primary input and output Model Content. Both are content-passthrough/transformation components that produce a modified or cached version of the input content.
Both perform Brep joining operations with a tolerance parameter and output a Brep. Brep Join Progression adds a 'compact' boolean but is otherwise functionally analogous to Brep Join with Tolerance.

Both sort/deduplicate geometry collections and output Unique items plus Indices. Sort Duplicate Curves operates on Curves while Sort Duplicate Breps operates on Breps, but the operation and output pattern are identical.
Both take a Surface input with Integer parameters and output a modified surface. Both perform surface modification operations (rebuilding vs reversing direction) with integer control parameters.

These two components form a pipeline pair: Create RTree produces an RTree output that is directly consumed as input by RTree Closest Point. They share the RTree data type and are semantically coupled as creator/consumer of the same spatial data structure.

Both take U and V integer parameters controlling resolution/degree in two directions and produce a surface-like output. Patch Surface uses curves as input while Rebuild Surface uses a Surface, but both are surface generation/modification tools with matching UV integer control pattern.

Identical input/output signatures (M: Geometry, L: Integer, S: NakedEdgeEnum → O: Geometry). Both are mesh subdivision algorithms with naked edge handling options, differing only in the subdivision algorithm applied (Catmull-Clark vs Split Polygons).

Identical input/output signatures (M: Geometry, L: Integer, S: NakedEdgeEnum → O: Geometry). Both are mesh subdivision algorithms with naked edge handling options, differing only in the subdivision algorithm applied (Catmull-Clark vs Loop).

Identical input/output signatures (M: Geometry, L: Integer, S: NakedEdgeEnum → O: Geometry). Both are mesh subdivision algorithms with naked edge handling options, differing only in the subdivision algorithm applied (Split Polygons vs Loop).

Identical input/output signatures (M: Geometry, L: Integer → O: Geometry) with no NakedEdgeEnum parameter. Both are simpler subdivision variants that do not expose naked edge handling, differing only in the subdivision pattern (Inner Polygons vs Sierpinski Triangles).

Share M: Geometry and L: Integer inputs and O: Geometry output. Both are Weaverbird subdivision components operating on mesh geometry with a level parameter; Catmull-Clark adds the NakedEdgeEnum option.
Share M: Geometry and L: Integer inputs and O: Geometry output. Both are Weaverbird subdivision components; Split Polygons adds the NakedEdgeEnum option.
Share M: Geometry and L: Integer inputs and O: Geometry output. Both are Weaverbird subdivision components; Loop adds the NakedEdgeEnum option.
Share M: Geometry and L: Integer inputs and O: Geometry output. Both are Weaverbird subdivision components; Catmull-Clark adds the NakedEdgeEnum option.
Share M: Geometry and L: Integer inputs and O: Geometry output. Both are Weaverbird subdivision components; Split Polygons adds the NakedEdgeEnum option.
Share M: Geometry and L: Integer inputs and O: Geometry output. Both are Weaverbird subdivision components; Loop adds the NakedEdgeEnum option.

Maximum and Minimum are direct analogs: both take two Generic Data inputs (A, B) and return a single Generic Data output (R). They perform complementary comparison operations and share identical parameter signatures.

Maximum and Extremes both take two Generic Data inputs (A, B) and perform comparison/ordering operations. Extremes outputs both min and max (V-, V+) while Maximum outputs only the max, making them closely related in purpose.
Minimum and Extremes both take two Generic Data inputs (A, B) and perform comparison/ordering operations. Extremes is essentially a combined Minimum+Maximum component.

Average and Weighted Average are direct analogs: both compute averages of Generic Data inputs and output AM (arithmetic mean). Weighted Average adds a weight parameter W but performs the same conceptual operation.

Complex Conjugate and Complex Modulus both operate on a single Complex input (C). They are complementary operations on complex numbers — conjugate returns a Complex, modulus returns a Number (magnitude).

Complex Conjugate and Complex Components both take a single Complex input (C). They are related complex number decomposition/transformation operations — one returns the conjugate Complex, the other decomposes into real (R) and imaginary (i) Number components.
Complex Modulus and Complex Components both take a single Complex input (C) and extract numerical information from it. Both are analysis/decomposition operations on complex numbers.

Create Complex and Complex Components are perfect inverses: Create Complex takes R (Number) and i (Number) to produce C (Complex), while Complex Components takes C (Complex) and outputs R (Number) and i (Number). They share all three parameter types.

Smooth Numbers and Blur Numbers both take Number input (N) and output Number (N), and both perform smoothing/averaging operations on number sequences. Blur Numbers has additional control parameters (S, I, L, W) but the core operation is analogous.

Truncate and Clamp both constrain/modify numeric values: Truncate cuts decimal places, Clamp restricts values to a domain. Both take a primary Generic Data input and a secondary constraint parameter, outputting constrained Generic Data.

Identical input/output signatures (Pln: Plane, Rad: Number, Trunc: Number -> Plato: Generic Data). Both are Platonic solid generators differing only in solid type (Octahedron vs Tetrahedron). Same parameter names and types throughout.

Identical input/output signatures (U, V: Integer; R, T, S: Number; D1, D2: Domain -> Srf: Generic Data). Both are parametric surface generators (Mobius vs Klein) with the same UV subdivision, scale, and domain parameters.
Identical input/output signatures. Both are parametric surface generators (Mobius vs Conoid) sharing all parameter names and types: U, V, R, T, S, D1, D2 -> Srf.
Identical input/output signatures. Both are parametric surface generators (Klein vs Conoid) sharing all parameter names and types: U, V, R, T, S, D1, D2 -> Srf.

Highly similar parametric surface generators sharing U, V (Integer), S (Number), D1, D2 (Domain) inputs and Srf output. Hyperbolic Paraboloid uses a, b instead of R, T but otherwise follows same UV+domain pattern.
Highly similar parametric surface generators sharing U, V (Integer), S (Number), D1, D2 (Domain) inputs and Srf output. Both generate mathematical surfaces with shape control parameters.
Highly similar parametric surface generators sharing U, V (Integer), S (Number), D1, D2 (Domain) inputs and Srf output. Both generate mathematical surfaces with shape control parameters.
Both are parametric surface generators sharing UV subdivision, S scale, D1/D2 domain inputs and Srf output. Enneper uses Integer 'a' for order parameter instead of Number R/T.
Both are parametric surface generators sharing UV subdivision, S scale, D1/D2 domain inputs and Srf output.
Both are parametric surface generators sharing UV subdivision, S scale, D1/D2 domain inputs and Srf output.
Both are parametric surface generators sharing UV subdivision, S scale, D1/D2 domain inputs and Srf output.

Both are parametric surface generators sharing U, V (Integer), S (Number), D1, D2 (Domain) inputs and Srf output. 3D Supershape has additional shape control parameters (m, a, b, n1, n2, n3) but follows same core pattern.
Both are parametric surface generators sharing U, V (Integer), S (Number), D1, D2 (Domain) inputs and Srf output. 3D Supershape extends the pattern with more shape parameters.
Both are parametric surface generators sharing U, V (Integer), S (Number), D1, D2 (Domain) inputs and Srf output.
Both are parametric surface generators sharing U, V (Integer), S (Number), D1, D2 (Domain) inputs and Srf output. Both use a, b as shape parameters.
Both are parametric surface generators sharing U, V (Integer), S (Number), D1, D2 (Domain) inputs and Srf output.
ArcCosine and ArcSine are both inverse trigonometric functions with identical Generic Data x->y signatures, operating on the same domain [-1,1] and returning angles
ArcCosine and ArcTangent are both inverse trigonometric functions with identical Generic Data x->y signatures, returning angle values
ArcSine and ArcTangent are both inverse trigonometric functions with identical Generic Data x->y signatures, returning angle values
Cosine and Sine are the two primary trigonometric functions, both with identical Generic Data x->y signatures, both take angle input and return ratio in [-1,1]
Cosine and Tangent are both primary trigonometric functions with identical Generic Data x->y signatures, taking angle input
Sine and Tangent are both primary trigonometric functions with identical Generic Data x->y signatures, taking angle input
Tangent and CoTangent are reciprocal trigonometric functions with identical Generic Data x->y signatures; CoTangent = 1/Tangent
Cosine and Secant are reciprocal trigonometric functions (Secant = 1/Cosine) with identical Generic Data x->y signatures
Sine and Sinc are closely related functions (Sinc = sin(x)/x) with identical Generic Data x->y signatures
Secant and CoTangent are both reciprocal trigonometric functions with identical Generic Data x->y signatures
Sinc and Cosine both share identical Generic Data x->y signatures and are closely related trigonometric-based functions
Sinc and Secant both share identical Generic Data x->y signatures as angle-based trigonometric functions
Degrees and Radians are exact inverse operations for angle unit conversion, both with Number->Number signatures; Degrees converts radians to degrees, Radians converts degrees to radians

Circumcentre and Orthocentre are both triangle geometry components with identical signatures (3 Point inputs -> Point + 3 Lines outputs), both compute special triangle center points and associated lines
ArcCosine and Cosine are inverse of each other, both with identical Generic Data x->y signatures
ArcSine and Sine are inverse of each other, both with identical Generic Data x->y signatures
ArcTangent and Tangent are inverse of each other, both with identical Generic Data x->y signatures
Sinc and CoTangent both share identical Generic Data x->y signatures as trigonometric-derived functions

Both are contour-generating components that slice geometry using a normal vector (N), distance (D), and produce Curve outputs. Contour takes generic Geometry while Point Cloud Contour targets point clouds, but the slicing concept and output type are identical.

Contour and Contour (ex) are direct variants of the same operation — both take Geometry and a distance D, and output Curve contours. Contour (ex) uses a Plane instead of Point+Vector but performs the same sectioning logic.

Both Point Cloud Contour and Contour (ex) are contour variants that produce Curve outputs with a distance/offset parameter D, performing analogous slicing operations on different input geometry types.

Brep | Plane and Mesh | Plane are direct analogs — both intersect a 3D geometry type (Brep vs Mesh) with a Plane and output intersection Curves. They share the same conceptual operation and I/O pattern differing only in geometry type.
Both Mesh | Plane and Contour (ex) use a Plane as a cutting/reference input and produce Curve outputs, performing section/intersection operations on geometry.
Both Brep | Plane and Contour (ex) take a Plane input and output Curves as section results, performing planar intersection/contour operations on solid geometry.

Curve | Line and Line | Plane both compute intersection/closest-point results and output a Point (P) and a parameter value (t/Number), representing the intersection location and its parametric position along the input geometry.
Curve | Line and Line | Line both compute closest-approach or intersection parameters, outputting parametric values (t/tA/tB) and Points (P/pA/pB). Both deal with linear geometry intersection math.
Line | Plane and Line | Line both take Line inputs and output parametric values (t/tA/tB) and intersection Points (P/pA/pB), performing analogous line-based intersection parameter computations.

Mesh | Ray and IsoVist Ray are both ray-casting operations that shoot a ray and return hit Points (P/X) and additional intersection data. Both involve a ray direction/line and geometry obstacles, computing ray-geometry intersection results.

Plane | Plane and Plane Region both take two Plane inputs (A/B or P/B) and compute a geometric result from their intersection/relationship — a Line or bounding Curve respectively. Both operate purely on plane pairs.
Both Group and Named Group take Geometry as input and produce a Group/Geometry output. Named Group extends Group by adding a Name parameter, making them analogous grouping operations.
Group and Ungroup are inverse operations sharing Group and Geometry types. Group takes Geometry and outputs Group; Ungroup takes Group and outputs Geometry — they are complementary pair operations.
Both Merge Group and Group produce a Group output. They both operate on grouping logic — one creates a group from geometry, the other merges two existing groups.

Both Transform and Inverse Transform operate on Transform type objects. Inverse Transform inverts a transform matrix, while Transform applies it — they are closely related transform manipulation operations sharing the Transform parameter type.
Both Split and Inverse Transform take a Transform as input and output a Transform. They both perform decomposition/manipulation of transform objects rather than applying them to geometry.
Both Split and Transform accept a Transform input. Split decomposes a transform while Transform applies it, making them related transform-handling components.

Spatial Deform (custom) and Spatial Deform are nearly identical: both take Geometry + Point (S) + Vector (F) and output Geometry. The custom variant adds a Text parameter for custom falloff expression, but the core IO pattern is the same.

Point Deform and Spatial Deform both deform geometry using point locations (P/S) and displacement vectors (M/F), outputting Geometry. They perform analogous point-based spatial deformation operations.
Point Deform and Spatial Deform (custom) share the same core deformation pattern: Geometry + Point + Vector → Geometry. Both perform point-driven spatial deformation of geometry.

Twist and Stretch both deform geometry along a Line axis (X) with a numeric parameter (A/L) and a Boolean for rigid/relative behavior (R), outputting Geometry. Both are axis-based deformation operations with similar parameter structures.

Twist and Taper both operate on geometry along a Line axis (X), share Boolean flags for infinite (I) and rigid (R) behavior, and output Geometry. Both are axis-based deformation transforms with shared control parameters.
Stretch and Taper both deform geometry along a Line axis (X) with numeric scale/ratio parameters and a Boolean rigid flag (R), outputting Geometry. Both are axis-based scaling/deformation operations.

Mirror Surface and Mirror Curve are analogous mirror operations: both take Geometry + a reference shape (Surface/Curve) + a Boolean toggle and output Geometry. They differ only in the mirror reference type (surface vs curve).

Box Morph and Surface Morph are analogous morphing operations: both take Geometry + a reference Box (R) and morph it into a target space (Twisted Box vs Surface with domain parameters), outputting Geometry. Both perform space-morphing deformations using a bounding box as source.

Blend Box and Surface Box both produce Twisted Box outputs from Surface + Domain² inputs. Surface Box adds a height parameter (H), while Blend Box uses two surface/domain pairs to blend between them. Both are Twisted Box constructors from surface parameters.

Blend Box and Twisted Box both output a Twisted Box. Blend Box derives it from two surfaces/domains, while Twisted Box constructs it explicitly from 8 corner points. Both are Twisted Box constructors used as inputs to Box Morph.
Surface Box and Twisted Box both produce Twisted Box outputs used as targets for Box Morph. They represent different construction methods for the same output type.
Sporph and Surface Morph both morph geometry onto target surfaces (S0/S1 vs S), take Geometry input, and output Geometry. Both perform surface-based space morphing with Boolean control parameters.

Box Morph and Sporph are both space-morphing operations that transform geometry from a reference space into a target space, outputting Geometry. Both use a reference bounding region and a Boolean for rigid behavior.

Both Create JSON and Write XML File share identical input signatures (Write: Boolean, Path: Text, DataSet: Generic Data) and both produce a file-format output (JSON or XML). They are analogous file-writing operations differing only in output format.

Both Create XML from Tree and Write XML File write XML output and share Write (Boolean) and Path (Text) inputs. Both produce XML Generic Data output. They differ in that Create XML from Tree takes a Tree input while Write XML File takes a DataSet.

Both Create XML from Tree and Create JSON share Write (Boolean) and Path (Text) inputs and both produce structured data file outputs. They are analogous serialization/file-writing operations for different formats (XML vs JSON).

Both Create Data Grid and Create DataTable share Headers (Text) and Values (Text) inputs and both produce tabular data structures. They are analogous operations for constructing grid/table data, differing mainly in output type naming and an additional Name input for DataTable.

Both Create CSV and Create DataTable share Headers (Text) and Values (Text) inputs and both organize data in tabular form. They are analogous data-creation components differing in output format (CSV vs DataTable).
Both Create Data Grid and Create CSV share Headers (Text) and Values (Text) inputs. They perform analogous operations of structuring tabular data, differing in output format (grid vs CSV).

Both Read CSV and Read XML by Tag are data-reading/parsing components that take a text-based data source input and produce multiple Generic Data outputs (Headers/Values vs InnerText/InnerXML). They are analogous read operations for different structured text formats.

Both Create DataSet and Create DataTable share a Name (Text) input and produce a single Generic Data output representing a named data container. They are analogous data-structure creation components at different levels of the data hierarchy (DataSet contains DataTables).

Pipe and Pipe Variable are direct variants: both take Curve C, Number R, Integer E (end type enum), Boolean Fr, and output Brep P. Pipe Variable adds a parameter t for variable radii but is otherwise identical in structure and purpose.

Sweep1 and Sweep2 are analogous sweep operations: both take rail curve(s) and section curve(s) and output a Brep. Sweep1 uses one rail, Sweep2 uses two rails. Both share the same fundamental sweep-along-rail paradigm and Brep output.

Sweep1 and Pipe both sweep a profile along a rail curve to produce a Brep. Pipe is essentially a specialized sweep with a circular cross-section. Both take a primary Curve input and output Brep, and both have integer parameters controlling sweep behavior.

Rail Revolution and Revolution are both revolution operations: both take a profile Curve P, an axis Line A, and output Brep S. Rail Revolution adds a rail curve R for guided revolution, while Revolution uses a Domain D for angular range. Analogous operations with nearly identical IO structure.

Ruled Surface and Sum Surface both take exactly two curve inputs (A and B) and produce a surface. Both create surfaces by interpolating between two curves, though by different mathematical methods (linear ruling vs. sum/translation).

Control Point Loft and Fit Loft are both loft variants: both take Curve C and Integer degree parameter(s) and output a Surface. They perform analogous lofting operations with different fitting strategies.

Control Point Loft and Loft both take curve inputs and produce lofted surfaces. They are variants of the same lofting operation, with Loft using a LoftOptions object for configuration and outputting Brep, while Control Point Loft uses degree directly.
Fit Loft and Loft are both loft operations taking curve inputs and producing surfaces/breps. They represent different approaches to the same lofting paradigm.

Edge Surface and Ruled Surface both create surfaces from curve boundary inputs and output Brep/Surface. Edge Surface takes 3-4 boundary curves while Ruled Surface takes exactly 2, but both construct surfaces defined entirely by curve edges.
Edge Surface and 4Point Surface both create surfaces from four boundary inputs (curves vs points respectively) and output a surface. Both define a surface patch from corner/edge geometry.
Sweep2 and Pipe both produce Brep outputs from curve inputs by sweeping a profile along rail curves. Pipe is a degenerate sweep with circular cross-section.

Both extrude geometry to produce Brep output. Extrude Linear takes Geometry+Line direction, Extrude Along takes Geometry+Curve path — both are extrusion operations producing Brep, differing only in how the extrusion direction/path is specified.

Both perform linear extrusion of geometry. Extrude Linear uses a Line axis with plane orientation, Extrude uses a Vector direction. Both take Geometry as primary input and produce extruded output (Brep/Geometry), making them functionally analogous extrusion operations.

Both extrude a Geometry (B) input to produce extruded output. Extrude Along uses a Curve path while Extrude uses a Vector direction. They share the same primary input parameter name 'B' for geometry and produce equivalent extrusion results.

Both take Curve inputs and produce Surface output. Network Surface uses U/V curve networks, Boundary Surfaces uses boundary curves — both are surface-creation operations driven by curves, sharing the curve-in/surface-out pattern.

Both produce Surface output and both have an Integer parameter (C for continuity in Network Surface, U for U-count in Surface From Points). Both are surface construction components that require discretization/continuity control via integer inputs.

Both are surface construction components that produce Surface output from geometric primitives (curves vs points). They represent analogous surface-from-boundary-data operations, both commonly used for filling/patching surfaces from input geometry.

Both create Angular Dimensions and share the same D (Angular Dimension), As (Model Annotation Style) inputs/outputs. Both take two geometry inputs (A, B) defining the angle and a reference point/line. They are analogous operations: one uses Points, the other uses Lines to define the angle.

Both share nearly identical parameter sets (Ms, Te, Di, Ar, Un, Le, To) for annotation style configuration. Annotation Style creates/defines a style while Annotation Style Overrides modifies an existing annotation object's style — analogous create vs. override operations with the same settings parameters.

Both are dimension annotation components that take two Point inputs (A, B) and a Model Annotation Style, producing a dimension object. Aligned Dimension measures linear distance between points; Angle Dimension (Points) measures angle between points — analogous dimensioning operations.

Both are dimension annotation components sharing Plane (P) and Model Annotation Style (As) inputs/outputs. Both produce a dimension object and operate on geometric inputs within a plane context — analogous linear vs. angular dimensioning.

Both are annotation settings components that follow the same pass-through pattern (settings object in/out plus individual parameters). Both contain multiple Integer enum-type parameters (Tf, Tr, Ar vs Lu, Lr, Zs, Ff, Au, Ar, Az) and Number parameters — analogous settings containers for tolerance vs. units configuration.

Both are annotation settings components with the same pass-through pattern. Both contain Integer enum parameters and Number parameters for fine-grained annotation control — analogous settings containers for text vs. tolerance configuration.

Both are annotation settings components following the same pass-through pattern with settings object in/out. Both have numerous Integer enum parameters and Number values — analogous settings containers for text vs. units configuration.

Both are annotation settings components with pass-through pattern (settings object in/out). Both contain Integer and Number parameters for annotation configuration — analogous arrow settings vs. tolerance settings containers.

Both create annotation geometry objects (Text Entity vs. Centermark) placed on a Plane with a Model Annotation Style. Both follow the same pattern of annotation object + Plane + As inputs/outputs — analogous annotation placement components.

Both deal with font/text styling. Model Font has Font (F) input/output with Integer style parameters (W, S), while Annotation Text Settings also has Font (F) input/output with Integer parameters (M, Mf, Ha, Va, Ft) — both configure typographic properties for annotations.

Both are annotation configuration components that follow a getter/setter pattern with mirrored inputs and outputs. Both deal with annotation display settings and both include Boolean, Number, and Integer typed parameters for controlling annotation appearance. They operate in the same Rhino annotation domain.

Both components operate on annotation objects. Angle Dimension (Arc) works with Angular Dimension geometry while Evaluate Annotation Text takes a Geometry annotation input. Both are concerned with extracting or manipulating annotation data from Rhino annotation objects.

Both components are in the rhino_annotations family and deal with annotation objects. Annotation Dimension Settings configures annotation style settings while Evaluate Annotation Text extracts text from annotation geometry. They share the annotation domain but have very different parameter profiles.

Curve Frames and Horizontal Frames are nearly identical: both take Curve + Integer N, both output Plane F and Number t. They differ only in the frame orientation algorithm (perpendicular-to-curve vs horizontal). Same signature, analogous operation.

Perp Frames and Curve Frames share the same output signature (Plane F, Number t) and both take a Curve and Integer N. Perp Frames adds an extra Boolean A for alignment, but the core pattern is identical — both generate frames along a curve at N locations.

Perp Frames and Horizontal Frames both generate oriented planes along a curve at N count positions, outputting Plane F and Number t. Perp Frames adds Boolean A; otherwise the pattern is the same frame-generation family.

Divide Curve and Divide By Deviation both take Curve + Integer N and output Point P, Vector T, and Number t. They perform analogous curve-division operations; Divide By Deviation adds a deviation Number d output and uses adaptive sampling, but the core IO pattern is shared.

Divide Curve and Divide Distance both divide a curve into points, outputting Point P, Vector T, and Number t. They differ in the division criterion (count N vs distance D), making them analogous operations with identical output signatures.

Divide By Deviation and Divide Distance both output Point P, Vector T, Number t from a Curve input. Both are curve-division strategies with different criteria (deviation-adaptive vs fixed distance), sharing the same output pattern.

Curve Contour and Contour (ex) are clearly analogous: both take a Curve and a distance/offset Number D, both output Point C and Number t (intersection/contour parameters). They differ in how the contour plane is specified (Point+Vector vs Plane+Offset), but perform the same contour-intersection operation.

Shatter and Dash Pattern both take a Curve and Number parameter(s) and output Curve segments. Shatter splits at parameter values t; Dash Pattern splits into dash/gap segments using lengths. Both are curve-splitting operations producing Curve outputs from Curve + Number inputs.

Both take Brep as primary input and output Curve + Point intersection results. Brep|Brep outputs {C: Curve, P: Point} and Brep|Curve outputs {C: Curve, P: Point} — identical output signature, same intersection paradigm with Brep geometry.
Both Brep|Brep and Surface|Curve output Curve and Point as primary intersection results. Surface|Curve adds UV and normal data but shares the core C+P output pattern with Brep|Brep.

Both Brep|Curve and Surface|Curve take a Curve as secondary input and output {C: Curve, P: Point}. They perform analogous surface/solid vs curve intersection operations with nearly identical output signatures.

Both Curve|Curve and Curve|Self take Curve input(s) and output Point + Number (parameter t) intersection results. Curve|Self is the self-intersection variant of Curve|Curve with the same output pattern of points and t-parameters.

Both Curve|Curve and Multiple Curves take Curve inputs and output Point + parameter Numbers (tA, tB) + Integer indices (iA, iB). Multiple Curves extends Curve|Curve to handle multiple curve intersections with the same output schema.
Both Curve|Self and Multiple Curves take Curve input and output intersection Points and t-parameter Numbers. Both deal with self or mutual curve intersection scenarios.

Both Mesh|Mesh and Mesh|Curve take Mesh as primary input and compute intersections. Mesh|Mesh outputs intersection Curves; Mesh|Curve outputs intersection Points. Both are mesh-based intersection operations.

Both Clash and Collision Many|Many perform collision/clash detection between geometry objects and output Integer indices identifying colliding pairs. Both are proximity/overlap detection components rather than pure geometric intersection.

Both Clash and Mesh|Mesh take two Mesh inputs (A and B) and analyze their geometric relationship. Clash outputs integer indices i, j for clashing pairs; Mesh|Mesh outputs intersection curves. Both operate on dual-mesh input scenarios.

Both Surface Split and Surface|Curve take a Surface + Curve as inputs. Surface|Curve computes intersection data while Surface Split uses curves to split the surface, but they share the same S+C input pattern and operate on surface-curve relationships.
Both Brep|Curve and Mesh|Curve take a Curve as secondary input and output intersection Points. They perform analogous solid/mesh vs curve intersection operations outputting point locations.

Both are file writers triggered by a Boolean 'Write' input, require a Text 'Path', and output Generic Data. Excel Writer extends Text Writer with additional data/heading/worksheet params but shares the same core write-to-file pattern.

Text Writer and Text Reader are complementary file I/O components sharing Boolean trigger and Text Path inputs. Both operate on text files at a given path; one writes, the other reads. Mirror-image operations on the same file type.
Excel Writer and Text Reader both use a Boolean trigger and a Text Path input to interact with files on disk. Both involve file I/O workflows with path-based targeting.

Object Bake and Object Save are nearly identical in structure: both triggered by a Boolean 'Bake', both accept Generic Data Objects, Text Layer, object name, object color, and layer color. Object Save adds Dir/File path params for saving to disk, but the core object-handling pattern is shared.

Launch Application and Rhino Command are both action-trigger components with a Boolean trigger and a single Text payload (path vs command string). Neither produces meaningful outputs — both fire side-effects in the Rhino/OS environment.
Launch Application and Text Writer share a Boolean trigger and Text Path input structure, and both output Generic Data. Both are 'execute on trigger' components that act on a file-system path.
Launch Application and Excel Writer share Boolean trigger, Text Path input, and Generic Data output. Both are triggered-action components that operate on a file path.

Area Moments and Volume Moments are nearly identical in structure: both take a single Geometry input and output a scalar (area/volume), centroid Point C, inertia Vector I, second moment Vector S, and gyration Vector G. They are the 2D vs 3D analogs of the same moment-of-inertia computation.

Area Moments is a superset of Area: both accept Geometry and output area Number A and centroid Point C. Area Moments additionally provides inertia vectors. They perform the same core area computation.

Volume Moments and Area both take Geometry and output a scalar quantity plus a centroid Point C. Volume Moments extends this with inertia data, but the core pattern (geometry in, measure + centroid out) is shared.

Evaluate Surface and Principal Curvature share identical inputs (Surface S, UV Point uv) and both output a Plane F plus directional Vectors. They are complementary surface-evaluation operations at the same UV location.

Evaluate Surface and Surface Curvature share the same inputs (Surface S, UV Point uv) and both output a Plane F. They both evaluate a surface at a UV parameter location, differing only in what additional quantities they compute.

Principal Curvature and Surface Curvature are nearly identical: same inputs (Surface S, UV Point uv), same Plane F output, and both output curvature-related Numbers. Principal Curvature gives k1/k2 with principal directions; Surface Curvature gives Gaussian G and Mean M curvature — two representations of the same surface curvature analysis.

Brep Closest Point and Surface Closest Point are direct analogs: both take a Point P and a geometry (Brep/Surface), and both output the closest Point P, a normal/UV Vector, and distance Number D. They perform the same closest-point query on different geometry types.

Brep Edges and Deconstruct Brep both take a single Brep input and decompose it into sub-geometry including Curve edges E. Brep Edges focuses on edge curves by type; Deconstruct Brep outputs faces, edges, and vertices — both are Brep decomposition operations.

Brep Edges and Brep Topology both take a single Brep and analyze its topological structure. Brep Edges extracts edge curves by adjacency type; Brep Topology outputs face-face, face-edge, and edge-face adjacency indices — both interrogate Brep topology.

Deconstruct Brep and Brep Topology both accept a single Brep and expose its internal structure. Deconstruct Brep gives geometric sub-objects; Brep Topology gives adjacency index arrays — complementary ways to analyze the same Brep structure.

Both compute convex hulls from Point inputs and output an index list (I: Integer). Convex Hull 3D outputs a Mesh hull while Convex Hull outputs Curve hulls, but they are 3D vs 2D analogues of the same operation. Both share the 'I' integer output representing point indices.

Both are Voronoi decomposition components taking Point inputs and a bounding region (Box vs Rectangle/Plane). 3D Voronoi and Voronoi (2D) are direct 3D/2D analogues performing the same spatial partitioning operation.

Both are Voronoi-related components taking Point and Box inputs. 3D Voronoi computes all cells while Voronoi Cell computes a single cell for a given point with neighbor points. Both share Point and Box inputs and produce volumetric Voronoi geometry.

Both are Voronoi components taking Point inputs and producing Voronoi cells/curves. Voronoi produces 2D curve cells while Voronoi Cell produces a 3D Brep cell. They share the same conceptual operation of Voronoi partitioning.

Both are Delaunay triangulation components taking Point inputs. Delaunay Mesh (2D) uses a Plane and outputs a Mesh, while 3D Delaunay outputs edges (Line) and connectivity (Integer). They are 2D/3D analogues of the same Delaunay algorithm.

Both take Point and Plane inputs for 2D spatial operations. Delaunay Mesh triangulates points on a plane while Convex Hull computes the convex boundary on a plane. Both are planar point-set geometry operations.

Both take Point, Plane, and Integer (G: grid resolution) inputs and perform spatial subdivision/proximity analysis. Proximity 2D outputs Lines and type integers while QuadTree outputs Curves and Points. Both use a plane-based 2D grid structure with integer resolution parameter.

Quad Remesh Settings and Quad Remesh are directly coupled components in the same workflow. Settings produces a 'Quad meshing settings' object consumed by Quad Remesh. They share the same domain (quad remeshing) and are designed to work together.

Both are remeshing components taking Geometry inputs and producing Mesh outputs. Quad Remesh produces quad meshes while TriRemesh produces triangle meshes. Both accept guide curves/features and iteration/quality parameters, performing analogous remeshing operations.

CreatePlankton and DeconstructPlankton are inverse operations in the Plankton mesh workflow. CreatePlankton converts a Mesh to a PlanktonMesh, while DeconstructPlankton breaks a PlanktonMesh into its components. They are direct analogues in the same data conversion pipeline.

Both take Point and Box/boundary inputs and produce curve-like outputs. Facet Dome outputs Curves (P) and a Surface from points within a box, while Voronoi outputs Curves from points within a rectangular boundary. Both perform point-based spatial partitioning producing curves.

Both take Point and Box inputs for 3D spatial operations. Facet Dome creates a dome structure within a box from points, while 3D Voronoi partitions a box volume using points. Both share the Point+Box input pattern for volumetric spatial geometry generation.

Both components share a Rectangle input parameter 'B' as their primary boundary/domain definition. Both are generative pattern algorithms operating within a rectangular region, producing geometric outputs (Curves vs Lines). They belong to the same mesh_triangulation family and perform analogous spatial subdivision/pattern generation operations, though Voronoi Groups outputs curves from point group seeds while Substrate outputs lines via a crack propagation simulation.

Both components work directly with Hatch Line objects. Model Hatch Line defines/edits individual hatch lines (spacing, direction, offset), while Model Hatch Pattern aggregates hatch lines into a named pattern. They share the Hatch Line type as a primary I/O, forming a compositional pair where HatchLine feeds into HatchPattern.

Model Hatch and Model Hatch Pattern both operate within the hatching domain. Model Hatch consumes a Model Hatch Pattern as input, and Model Hatch Pattern produces one as output, making them semantically coupled. Both share the Model Hatch Pattern type as a key parameter.

Both components are part of the hatch definition pipeline. Model Hatch Line defines low-level hatch geometry while Model Hatch applies hatching to surfaces. Both share a Number scale/spacing parameter (S) and operate within the same hatching workflow.

Both components operate on Model Linetype objects. Query Model Linetypes retrieves existing linetypes by name pattern, while Model Linetype defines/edits linetype properties. They share the Model Linetype type as primary I/O and both involve linetype name (N/Text) parameters, forming a query-then-edit pattern.

Both Model Linetype and Model Hatch Pattern are named model definition objects with similar structural patterns: both have a Text name (N), a scale/spacing Number (S), and sub-element lists (segments vs hatch lines). They follow the same model object definition pattern.

Model Hatch accepts a Colour Gradient (Fs) and Colour (Bc) for fill styling. Colour Gradient defines gradient properties with Points (S, E) and Number (R). They share the Colour Gradient type as a linking parameter, with Model Hatch consuming what Colour Gradient produces.

Both Sphere and Quad Sphere take identical inputs (Plane B, Number R) and produce a spherical geometry output (Surface vs Brep). They are direct analogs performing the same conceptual operation with different output representations.
Cylinder and Cone share identical inputs (Plane B, Number R, Number L) and both output a Surface C. They are analogous revolution-based primitives defined by a base plane, radius, and length/height.
Sphere and Cylinder both take a Plane B and Number R as inputs and output a Surface. Both are revolution-based primitives defined by a base plane and radius.
Sphere and Cone both take a Plane B and Number R as inputs and output a Surface. Both are revolution-based primitives defined by a base plane and radius.

Center Box and Domain Box both take a Plane B and output a Box B. Both define a box from a base plane with dimensional parameters, differing only in whether dimensions are given as Numbers or Domains.
Center Box and Box 2Pt both output a Box B. They are analogous box construction methods — one from a center plane with X/Y/Z extents, the other from two corner points with an optional plane.
Domain Box and Box 2Pt both output a Box B. They are alternative methods for constructing boxes — one using domain ranges on a plane, the other using two corner points.

Plane Surface and Domain Box share the same input pattern (Plane, Domain X, Domain Y) — Plane Surface stops at 2D while Domain Box adds a Z domain. Both define geometry extents using domains on a plane.
Cylinder and Quad Sphere share a Plane B and Number R input. Both are solid-like primitives defined by a base plane and radius, producing closed geometry outputs.

Both are remeshing components that take Geometry, a target length, Curve creases/constraints, and Point corners/vertices as inputs, producing a remeshed result. remesher adds flip/pull/iter/reset for interactive simulation while SimpleRemesh uses Steps, but the core remeshing pattern is nearly identical.

Both Refine and RefineStrips take a Mesh and an Integer level L as inputs and output a refined Mesh. They perform analogous subdivision/refinement operations on mesh topology, differing only in that RefineStrips targets strip-based mesh structures.
Both Refine and ByParent share identical input/output signatures (Mesh + Integer L → Mesh), performing mesh subdivision or grouping operations controlled by an integer parameter.
RefineStrips and ByParent share identical I/O signatures (Mesh + Integer L → Mesh), both operating on mesh topology with an integer control parameter.
Both Diagonalize and Combine&Clean take a single Mesh input and output a single Mesh, performing topology-modifying operations on the mesh without additional parameters.
Both Diagonalize and MeshDirection take a single Mesh input and output a single Mesh, performing structural or orientation modifications on the mesh without additional parameters.
Both Combine&Clean and MeshDirection share identical I/O signatures (Mesh → Mesh), performing single-input mesh processing operations with no additional parameters.
Both HingePoints and Bipartite take only a Mesh as input and perform analysis/decomposition operations on mesh topology, extracting structural properties (hinge geometry vs. bipartite coloring).

Both are 'Query Model' components that take a Text Pattern (N) as input and return a single model object type (Model Layer vs Model Block Definition). They share the same query-by-name pattern and analogous roles in querying different model object types.

Both components operate on Model Block Definitions (Bd) as a primary parameter and pass them through as outputs. They share the Bd input/output pattern and are both concerned with block definition management (instantiation vs export).

Both components follow a passthrough pattern where the primary model object (Block Instance vs Model Layer) is passed in and returned unchanged alongside modifier parameters. Both have Boolean outputs and act as property-setting wrappers around model objects.

Both deal with Model Block Definitions and Model Layers respectively — analogous model object types. Query Model Block Definitions produces Bd objects consumed by Model Block Instance and Export, while Hide Model Layer operates on Model Layer objects produced by Query Model Layers, forming parallel query-then-operate patterns.

Both RigidBody and RigidPointSet define rigid constraints in Kangaroo2, sharing Plane, Points, and Strength inputs and outputting a Generic Data goal object (RB). They perform analogous operations of defining rigid configurations from point sets with a reference plane.

Both SolidPlaneCollide and RigidBody are Kangaroo2 goals that take a Plane input and Strength parameter, outputting a Generic Data goal. Both define physical interaction/constraint behaviors for simulation objects.

Both SolidPlaneCollide and Support are Kangaroo2 goals involving Plane inputs and Strength parameter, outputting Generic Data. Both define constraint/collision behaviors in simulation with a strength weighting.
Both RigidBody and Support are Kangaroo2 constraint goals sharing Plane and Strength inputs with Generic Data output. Both constrain the motion of simulation elements relative to reference frames.

Both Support and RigidPointSet are Kangaroo2 goals with Plane and Strength inputs and Generic Data output. Both define positional/rotational constraints anchoring simulation elements to target frames.
Both are object-level display/print attribute selectors (linetype vs print colour) with identical no-input picker pattern, used to assign per-object overrides in Rhino model context
Both are object-level attribute pickers (linetype vs display mode) applied per-object as overrides, same structural pattern with no inputs
Both are object-level visual attribute selectors (print colour vs display mode) with no inputs, used as per-object overrides in the same workflow

Both deal with display modes - Model Display Mode picks a viewport-level display mode while Object Display Mode picks a per-object display mode override; nearly identical picker pattern and output type
Both are viewport selector components (Layout Viewport vs Model Viewport) with identical no-input picker pattern, analogous operations for different viewport contexts
Both are annotation-related settings components (Arrow Settings vs Leader Settings) with no inputs; leaders use arrows, so they share overlapping annotation configuration concerns
Both are annotation settings components (Arrow Settings vs Dimension Settings) with no inputs; dimensions use arrows, making them closely related annotation configuration components
Both are annotation settings selectors (Leader Settings vs Dimension Settings) with no inputs; both configure annotation object appearance in the model annotation style context
Both are annotation settings components (Text Settings vs Dimension Settings) with no inputs; both configure sub-properties of annotation styles
Both are annotation settings components (Text Settings vs Leader Settings) with no inputs; leaders contain text, making these closely related annotation sub-setting pickers
Model Annotation Style is the parent container for Arrow, Leader, Text, and Dimension settings; structurally identical no-input picker pattern operating in the same annotation domain
Model Annotation Style encompasses Text Settings as a sub-property; both are annotation-domain no-input pickers in the same family
Model Annotation Style encompasses Dimension Settings; both are annotation-domain no-input pickers operating at different levels of the annotation style hierarchy
Both are settings selector components (Tolerance Settings vs Dimension Settings) with no inputs; dimension tolerances bridge these two domains making them semantically adjacent
Both are model-level resource pickers (Hatch Pattern vs Linetype) with no inputs; both select named model resources used to style geometry display
Both are model-level object/definition pickers (Block Definition vs Model Object) with no inputs; block definitions are composed of model objects, making them closely related model database selectors
Both are Rhino model property parameter components (Material vs Layer) with identical empty I/O structure, serving as model attribute selectors
Both are Rhino model attribute parameter components (Material vs Attribute Key) with identical empty I/O structure
Both are Rhino model parameter components (Material vs Action) with identical empty I/O structure
Both are Rhino model parameter components (Material vs Content) with identical empty I/O structure
Both are Rhino model attribute parameter components (Layer vs Attribute Key) with identical empty I/O structure, both relate to object organization/metadata
Both are Rhino model parameter components (Layer vs Action) with identical empty I/O structure
Both are Rhino model parameter components (Layer vs Content) with identical empty I/O structure
Both are Rhino model attribute/action parameter components with identical empty I/O structure
Both are Rhino model attribute parameter components (Attribute Key vs Content) with identical empty I/O structure
Both are Rhino model parameter components (Action vs Content) with identical empty I/O structure
Both are Rhino object property parameter components (Print Width vs Layer) with identical empty I/O structure, both relate to object display/organization properties
Both are Rhino object display property parameter components (Print Width vs Material) with identical empty I/O structure
Both are Rhino object property parameter components (Print Width vs Content) with identical empty I/O structure

Both are Laplacian-based mesh smoothing algorithms sharing Geometry input (M), iteration count (L), naked edge handling enum (S), and Geometry output (O). LaplacianHC is an extension of Laplacian Smoothing with additional bias/offset parameters (P, O, A) but the core operation and parameter structure are nearly identical.

Both perform iterative mesh smoothing operations sharing Geometry input (M), iteration count (L), strength/weight number (T), and Geometry output (O). LaplacianHC adds NakedEdgeEnum and extra numeric params, while Blur Mesh is a simpler smoothing variant without naked edge control.

Both are iterative mesh smoothing operations sharing identical core parameters: Geometry input (M), iteration count (L), smoothing strength number (T), and Geometry output (O). Laplacian Smoothing adds NakedEdgeEnum (S) for boundary control, but the fundamental smoothing pattern is the same as Blur Mesh.

Both find closest points among a set: Closest Point (P, C→P, i, D) and Closest Points (P, C, N→P, i, D) share identical output signatures (closest point, index, distance) and nearly identical inputs. Closest Points adds N for returning multiple nearest neighbors.

Both perform closest-point queries returning (Point, Index, Distance). Closest Point queries a list of points; Point Cloud Closest Point queries a point cloud. Analogous operations on different data structures with identical output patterns.

Both are closest-point search components returning (Point, Index, Distance). Closest Points searches a point list; Point Cloud Closest Point searches a point cloud. Same output signature and analogous operation.
Construct Point (X, Y, Z → Pt) and Deconstruct (P → X, Y, Z) are exact inverses. They share the same X/Y/Z number parameters and point, making them a natural construct/deconstruct pair.

Both sort points and return sorted points with reorder indices (P→P, I). Sort Points sorts by coordinates; Sort Along Curve sorts by curve parameter. Same output signature (Point list + Integer index list), analogous sorting operation.

Both operate on point lists and return filtered/sorted point sets with integer index mappings. Sort Points returns sorted points + indices; Cull Duplicates returns culled points + original indices + valence. Related point-list processing operations.

Both construct a Point from numeric coordinate inputs. Construct Point uses Cartesian (X, Y, Z); Point Cylindrical uses cylindrical coordinates (Angle, Radius, Elevation) with a reference Plane. Analogous coordinate-system point constructors.

Point Cylindrical converts cylindrical coords to a Point; To Polar converts a Point to polar coordinates. Both involve cylindrical/polar coordinate systems with a Plane reference and numeric angle/radius parameters — inverse coordinate-conversion operations.

Both compute distances between points. Distance (A, B → D) gives scalar distance; Closest Point (P, C → P, i, D) also outputs distance D. Both take point inputs and produce a distance number, with Closest Point extending to also identify which point is nearest.

Both produce a Point from numeric inputs. Construct Point uses 3 Cartesian numbers; Barycentric uses 3 reference points and 3 weight numbers (U, V, W). Both are point constructors from numeric parameters, with Barycentric being a weighted interpolation variant.

Both project/find points on geometry and return a point result with an integer index. Project Point (P, D, G → P, I) projects onto geometry; Closest Point (P, C → P, i, D) finds nearest point. Both map input points to geometry-derived output points with index tracking.

Both components take Point inputs and produce Number and Integer outputs. Point Groups clusters points by distance (D), while Pull Point finds closest geometry and returns distance (D) and index (I). Both operate on point sets and yield proximity/grouping metrics.

Both components produce Point outputs. Point Groups outputs grouped points, while Point Polar constructs a point from polar coordinates. Both are point-centric but differ significantly in operation and input structure.

Both produce Point outputs. Pull Point returns the closest point on geometry, while Point Polar constructs a point in 3D polar coordinates. Both deal with point positioning but serve very different purposes.

Both Mesh Sphere and Mesh Sphere Ex take a Plane (B) and Number (R) as inputs and output a Mesh (M). They are variants of the same sphere mesh operation, differing only in subdivision control (U/V counts vs single count C).

Both Mesh Triangle and Mesh Quad take Integer vertex index inputs and output a Mesh face (F). They are analogous face construction components differing only in the number of vertices (3 vs 4), and both feed into Construct Mesh.
Both Mesh Sphere and Mesh Box take multiple Integer subdivision parameters (U/V vs X/Y/Z) and output a Mesh (M). Both are primitive mesh generators with resolution control.
Both Mesh Sphere and Mesh Plane take Integer subdivision parameters and output a Mesh (M). Both are parametric primitive mesh generators with resolution/count control.
Both Mesh Sphere Ex and Mesh Box take Integer count/subdivision inputs and output a Mesh (M). Both are compact primitive mesh generators.
Construct Mesh consumes Mesh face (F) output from Mesh Triangle and Mesh Quad. They form a natural pipeline: face constructors feed into Construct Mesh to build complete meshes.
Construct Mesh consumes Mesh face (F) output from Mesh Quad. Analogous pipeline relationship as with Mesh Triangle — both quad and triangle faces feed Construct Mesh.

CoCircular and CoLinear share identical input/output signatures (Points: Point, Strength: Number → C: Generic Data) and both are Kangaroo2 geometric constraint goals operating on point sets with a strength parameter.

CoCircular and CoPlanar share identical input/output signatures (Points: Point, Strength: Number → C: Generic Data) and both are Kangaroo2 geometric constraint goals that enforce a geometric co-relationship among points with a strength parameter.

CoLinear and CoPlanar share identical input/output signatures (Points: Point, Strength: Number → C: Generic Data) and both are Kangaroo2 geometric constraint goals enforcing collinearity/coplanarity among point sets with a strength parameter.

Both Text Split and Text Join are inverse operations on text lists: Split breaks text into parts using a delimiter, Join combines text parts with a joiner. Both take Text inputs and produce Text outputs, and are natural complements often used together.

Text Join and Concatenate both combine multiple text inputs into a single text output. Both take Text inputs and produce Text output R. They differ in that Join uses a separator and works on lists, while Concatenate appends A+B directly, but the operation is analogous.

Replace Text and Text Split both operate on a primary Text input T with a secondary Text pattern/delimiter input, producing Text output. Both perform string manipulation by locating substrings within text.

Format and Concatenate both produce a single Text output by combining or formatting multiple inputs. Format uses a format string template while Concatenate directly appends, but both serve the purpose of assembling text from components.

Text Fragment and Text Split both extract subsets of text from a primary Text input T, producing Text output. Fragment uses index and length (integer params) to extract a substring, while Split divides by delimiter — both are text extraction/decomposition operations.

Match Text and Replace Text both take a primary Text input T and a pattern Text input P/F, operating on substring matching. Both deal with finding patterns within text strings and have a case-sensitivity or replacement consideration.

Characters and Text Fragment both decompose text at a granular level: Characters splits text into individual character units with their unicode values, while Text Fragment extracts a substring by position. Both analyze the internal structure of text.

Format and Text Join both assemble multiple inputs into a single Text output using a template/separator string (F for Format, J for Join). Both use a secondary Text parameter to control how the inputs are combined.
Bevel Edges and Mesh Window share identical I/O signatures (M: Geometry, D: Number, T: InsetTypeEnum -> O: Geometry) and both perform inset-type mesh face operations with the same enum parameter type
Bevel Edges and Picture Frame share identical I/O signatures (M: Geometry, D: Number, T: InsetTypeEnum -> O: Geometry) and both perform inset-type mesh operations
Bevel Edges and Sierpinski Carpet share identical I/O signatures (M: Geometry, D: Number, T: InsetTypeEnum -> O: Geometry) and both use InsetTypeEnum for face subdivision operations
Mesh Window and Picture Frame share identical I/O signatures and both create frame/window-like inset patterns on mesh faces using InsetTypeEnum
Mesh Window and Sierpinski Carpet share identical I/O signatures (M: Geometry, D: Number, T: InsetTypeEnum -> O: Geometry)
Picture Frame and Sierpinski Carpet share identical I/O signatures (M: Geometry, D: Number, T: InsetTypeEnum -> O: Geometry)

Offset Mesh and Mesh Thicken share identical I/O signatures (M: Geometry, D: Number, T: OffsetTypeEnum -> O: Geometry) and both perform offset/thickening operations using the same OffsetTypeEnum parameter
Offset Mesh and Bevel Edges share the same M/D/O parameter structure and both perform geometric offset-style transformations on meshes; differ only in enum type (OffsetTypeEnum vs InsetTypeEnum)
Offset Mesh and Mesh Window share the same M/D/O parameter structure and both use an enum type for mesh transformation mode selection
Offset Mesh and Picture Frame share the same M/D/O parameter structure and both use an enum type for mesh transformation mode selection
Offset Mesh and Sierpinski Carpet share the same M/D/O parameter structure and both use an enum type for mesh transformation mode selection
Mesh Thicken and Bevel Edges share the same M/D/O parameter structure; both apply a distance-based mesh transformation with an enum type parameter
Mesh Thicken and Mesh Window share the same M/D/O parameter structure and both use an enum type for mesh transformation mode selection
Mesh Thicken and Picture Frame share the same M/D/O parameter structure and both use an enum type for mesh transformation mode selection
Mesh Thicken and Sierpinski Carpet share the same M/D/O parameter structure and both use an enum type for mesh transformation mode selection
Stellate/Cumulation and Offset Mesh both take Geometry+Number inputs and produce Geometry output; both perform distance-based mesh transformations, though Stellate lacks the enum type parameter
Stellate/Cumulation and Mesh Thicken both take Geometry+Number inputs and produce Geometry output; both perform distance-based mesh transformations
Stellate/Cumulation and Bevel Edges both perform distance-based mesh subdivision/transformation operations producing Geometry output; Stellate lacks the enum type and has no Geometry input for M
Bevel Vertices and Bevel Edges share the same D/T/O parameter pattern and InsetTypeEnum, and both perform beveling operations; differ in that Bevel Vertices takes Boolean for M instead of Geometry
Bevel Vertices and Mesh Window share D/T/O parameter pattern and InsetTypeEnum; both perform inset-type mesh face operations
Bevel Vertices and Picture Frame share D/T/O parameter pattern and InsetTypeEnum
Bevel Vertices and Sierpinski Carpet share D/T/O parameter pattern and InsetTypeEnum
Both Scalar Display and Tensor Display share identical input signatures (Field, Rectangle, Integer) and perform field visualization/display operations over a sampled grid.

Scalar Display and Direction Display are nearly identical: same inputs (F: Field, S: Rectangle, N: Integer) and same output (D: Mesh). Both visualize a field over a rectangular domain as a mesh, differing only in what field property they display (scalar magnitude vs. direction).

Tensor Display and Direction Display share identical input signatures (Field, Rectangle, Integer) and both perform field visualization over a sampled rectangular domain, analogous display operations on different field aspects.

Mesh Prism and Mesh Pyramid share identical input signatures (P, W, S, T, C, F) and identical Mesh output. Both are prismatic solid mesh generators with tessellation control, differing only in geometry (prism vs pyramid shape).

Mesh Prism and Mesh Antiprism share identical input signatures (P, W, S, T, C, F) and identical Mesh output. Both are rotationally symmetric solid mesh generators with tessellation control, with antiprism being a close variant of prism.

Mesh Pyramid and Mesh Antiprism share identical input signatures (P, W, S, T, C, F) and identical Mesh output. Both generate n-sided solid meshes with tessellation control from a plane and size parameter.

Mesh Dipyramid and Mesh Prism share most inputs (P, W, S, T, C) and Mesh output. Dipyramid lacks the TessellationEnum F input but is otherwise structurally analogous as an n-sided solid mesh generator.

Mesh Dipyramid and Mesh Pyramid share most inputs (P, W, S, T, C) and Mesh output. Both are pyramid-family solids (dipyramid is a double pyramid), differing mainly by the absence of TessellationEnum in Dipyramid.
Mesh Dipyramid and Mesh Antiprism share most inputs (P, W, S, T, C) and Mesh output. Both are n-sided solid mesh generators placed on a plane, with Dipyramid lacking the TessellationEnum parameter.
Mesh Icosahedron and Mesh Dipyramid both generate Mesh output from Plane and Number inputs. Icosahedron is a simpler fixed-topology solid while Dipyramid has additional side-count and apex controls.
Mesh Icosahedron and Mesh Prism share Plane and Number inputs with Mesh output. Both generate platonic/prismatic solid meshes from a plane and size, with Prism having additional topology controls.
Mesh Icosahedron and Mesh Pyramid share Plane and Number inputs with Mesh output. Both are solid mesh generators placed on a plane with a size parameter.
Mesh Icosahedron and Mesh Antiprism share Plane and Number inputs with Mesh output. Both generate symmetric solid meshes from a plane and size parameter.

Both are 'remove duplicate' operations sharing identical parameter structure: a geometry input (L/P) and a numeric tolerance (t), outputting filtered geometry (Q). They perform the same logical operation (deduplication) on different geometry types (Lines vs Points), making them highly analogous siblings.

Both take a Curve (Line), a Number for length/target length, and a Strength Number, outputting a Generic Data goal. Length(Line) sets a target length while PlasticLength sets a plastic rest length — analogous length-constraint goals with identical IO structure.

Both take a Curve, a Number parameter (Length vs Factor), and Strength, outputting a Generic Data goal. Both are length-targeting constraints on lines — LengthSnap snaps to multiples of a factor, Length sets an absolute target.
Both take a Curve, a single Number (L vs Factor), and Strength, outputting a Generic Data goal. Both are length-modifying goals that adjust rest or snap length of a line element.

Both take a Curve and Strength Number, outputting Generic Data. Both are length-related goals on line/curve elements — ClampLength constrains within bounds while Length(Line) targets a specific length.
Both take a Curve and Strength, outputting Generic Data. Both are length-constraint goals operating on curves/lines with a strength parameter.
Both take a Curve and Strength, outputting Generic Data. Both are length-modifying goals — ClampLength clamps to a range, LengthSnap snaps to a factor.
Both take a Curve and Strength Number, outputting Generic Data. EqualLength enforces equal lengths among lines while Length(Line) targets a specific length — both are length equality/target goals.
Both take a Curve and Strength, outputting Generic Data. Both are length-constraint goals on line elements.
Both take a Curve and Strength, outputting Generic Data. Both are length-related Kangaroo2 goals operating on curve inputs.
Both take a Curve and Strength, outputting Generic Data. EqualLength and ClampLength are both length-constraint goals with the same core IO pattern.
Both take a Curve and a single Number (W vs Strength), outputting Generic Data. Both are simple line-based Kangaroo2 goals with minimal parameters.

Both take Line inputs and a Strength Number, outputting Generic Data. Both are directional/relational goals operating on Line geometry rather than Curve, distinguishing them from the other length-based components.

Both are anchor-type goal components: AnchorXYZ and Anchor both take a Point P and Strength Number, output Generic Data A. They perform the same conceptual operation (anchoring a point) with slightly different parameterizations — AnchorXYZ uses boolean axis locks while Anchor uses a target point T.

Both AnchorXYZ and PlasticAnchor are anchor-type goals taking Point P and Strength Number, outputting Generic Data A. They share the anchor goal pattern but differ in constraint type (axis-locked vs plastic/yielding behavior).

Both Anchor and PlasticAnchor are anchor-type goal components taking Point P and Strength Number, outputting Generic Data A. They share the same structural I/O pattern and perform analogous anchoring operations with different mechanical behaviors.

Both Floor and FloorFriction are floor-type goal components that output Generic Data representing a floor constraint. Floor is a simplified version (only Strength), while FloorFriction adds Point P, Level L, and Slip S parameters. They are analogous collision/constraint goals for ground planes.

Both MagnetSnap and Bomb take a Points (Point) input and a Strength Number, outputting Generic Data. They both operate on collections of points with a radius/detonation range parameter (R vs Detonation), performing force-based interactions on point sets.

Both AnchorXYZ and MagnetSnap take Point and Strength Number inputs and output Generic Data. Both are positional constraint goals that pull points toward target locations, differing in that MagnetSnap operates on a radius-based snap while AnchorXYZ uses axis locks.

Both Transform and Anchor take Point inputs and a Strength Number, outputting Generic Data. Both define positional goals that move points toward a target state, with Transform adding a Transform matrix for more complex repositioning.

Both are query components that take a Text Pattern input (N) and output view-related content (Model Content vs Model Viewport). They perform analogous filtering/querying operations on different view types (named views vs viewports) in the Rhino model.
